THE CARRIER-DOVE. "No place like home !" it is truly said; Wherever I rest or roam • There shines no light like the sweet light shed By the sun and stars of home. "Fly away! fly away! fly away, dove! Over the shore and sea! Fly away, dove, to the home I love, With a message to mine from me r And my message of love to the dove I tied, And I wrote, "Wherever I roam, There is never a hearth like my own fireside, Or a love like the loves of home." Then "Home" to the dove I whispered," Fly!" And it rose and it floated away, Tin it died in the light of the sunset sky, And the bourne of the dying day. And I thought that the sunset gold of heaven Fell on its wings as it flew, As bright as the light of a star is given To a flower that sleeps in the dew. Was it the light of heaven, sweet dove, That guided your white wings home? • Was there a voice in the breeze of love, That whispered you whither to roam? ' Ah! who can tell? I only know On high is a Spirit of Love; " I only know to our earth below - .221.144.0 14,1.4 . It descended like a dove. r Like a sweet white dove from its home on high, Which earth shall retain in vain, For the spirit., I know, to its home in the sky, Like a dove, will return again. Yes, yes • when the sunset of life is near, And the sky is a golden smile, And the clouds, in its sea of light, appear • Like many a golden isle— (For I love to picture life's sunset thus, For the sky was even so When the dove, on its pinions glorious, Flew home in the sunset's glow)— I shall gaze on the sunset sky overhead, And think of the Spirit of Love. And say, "Home, spirit! home !" as I said "Home !" to the carrier-dove. —Rey. S. K. Cowan, MA. Girl's Olen Paper.

Governor Porter of Indiana is noted for his childlike and bland methods when he goes out to speak during an election tour. He always assumes the familiarity of knowing all people. On one occasion he went down to Franklin, twenty miles below Indianapolis. He rose to speak with his face wreathed in smiles, and began, "Ladies and gentlemen, it affords me great pleasure to meet my old friends whom I have known so long." At this point some shrill voice in the audience shouted, "Name 'em—name 'em, governor." This so discon- certed the governor that he did not recover from it the whole evening. DODGING THE Issuz.—He was a slow coach. Her mother said so; the old man said so; her big brother said so, and scowled darkly when he threatened to call him to account. The reason of all this was that he had long hesitated to pop the question. He and she were sitting in the' gloaming. She said: "Alfonso, were you ever engaged ?" " Yessum," was the sad and unex- pected reply. She winced, but immediately rallied, and continued: "Did the adored one cruelly break her plighted troth ?" "No ; I severed my connection." "0, you cruel-hearted flirt!" "Yes; the firm I was engaged with heartlessly bounced me." "0, a firm—your em- ployers! And for why, Alphonsy ?" she said, snuggling closer to him on the rustic bench. Alphonso hitched a little nearer off, and replied gloomily: "For mental in- capacity." "0, no, say not so," said the girl; "you are not ignorant." "Yes, I am," said Alphonso, "I'm a howling idiot." "0, no ; you are keen, young, bright, and intellectual. You have a future before you to be shared by some warm and loving heart." "No; the future is all a blank— blank as my own vacant mind. On the body politic I'm but a wart.' "Think of the happy home you might rear for yourself and—and--" "No. lam such a blamed fool, I never accumulate enough property to put in tea. Financially I am a total wreck, and intellectually busted from away back. Physically, I'm nothing but a shell." "0, say not so, Alphonsy." "If I only had a cheap, second-hand throne, my fractured reason would be sure to totter and wobble all over IL" "But papa says you are quite a successful speculator." "That's where the old man is off." "And mamma says you own a fine house." "The good woman errs. I'm penniless." "And my big brother declares that unless you mean business, and your intentions are honourable, that he proposes to horsewhip you on sight in the most prominent street in town, and that you have got either to cash up or draw out of the game."—Alphonso is now a happy husband and father.

MIES OF THE Bnica—ln early times not only did the Birch provide primitive man with his canoe, but it pro- bably roofed his rude shanty, and furnished fibre for his cable, fishing-lines, or other cordage, in districts beyond the northern limit of the Linden. Probably, too it was at no late period in the history of civilisation that man took to tapping the white trunks in the spring for the sake of the copious flow of sugary sap, and to ferment- ing this sap into a wine or spirit, as is still done both in Sweden and in Leicestershire. It is a remarkable fact in sociology that there is hardly a country in the world that has not some alcoholic drink, and also some more innocuous infusion containing a vegetable alkaloid, similar to the theme, caffeine, and theobromine of our tea, coffee, and cocoa. Besides a beer, prepared formerly from its young shoots, the Birch yields beverages of both these classes; the wine just men- tioned, and a tea prepared from the leaves, chiefly by the Finlanders. The bark, moreover, contains enough starch to furnish, when bruised, a bread-stuff to the Samoiedes and Kamtschadales. It is also still used in the north for roofing, being very durable and imperme- able, and in Russia for the manufacture of jars, boxes, and shoes, and for tanning. On distillation, it yields a fragrant oil, which gives its pleasant odour to Russian leather. The wood, though not durable, is valued in Russia, where the birch forms the chief tree in vast forest areas, not only as fire-wood and as a source of charcoal, but also, on account of its tougkness and tena- city, for carriage-building, furniture, and turnery. A very extensive domestic industry in that country is the manufacture of wooden spoons; thirty millions, meetly of birchweod, being made annually. The flexible branches are largely utilised in the making of brooms, and it is stated that the "fasces" carried by the " lictors" before the magistrates of ancient Rome were made up of birch-rods. We may doubt the exact truth of the statement made by M. Alphonse Karr, in his charming " Tour autour demon Jardin," that "in London they make champagne from " the Birch; but no schoolboy will probably dispute the truth of his further statement. that "the most virtuous uses to which it is applied are brooms arid wooden shoes." Nevertheless, Dr. Turner, the pugnacious Dean of Wells, is of a dif- ferent opinion, for in his" Herball" (1568) he writes of it: "I have not red of any vertue it bath in physick ; how- beit, it serveth for many good uses, and for none better than for betynge of stubborn boys, that either lye or will not learn." This, too, is the only connection in which Shakspeare refers to this beautiful tree. In Measure for Measure he tells how fond fathers—

Hating bound up the threatening twigs of Birch, Only to stick it in their children's sight For terror, not to use, in time the rod Becomes more mocked than feared. 7—From "Familiar Trees 'liar April. THE MOST ANCIENT WOOD ENGIIATINGS.—AIthough carving in wood was practiced by almost all nations, in some form, at an early date, it only became an art when means were invented to obtain printed impressions from raised surfaces, such as the block-printing of China, and the similar manufacture of playing cards in Europe. Card-makers and figure cutters are mentioned as a class in the Low Countries at the beginning of the fifteenth century. The figure of St. Christopher, with the date of 1423, was for s long time considered the earliest engraving from wood with an ascertained date; but a picture was afterwards found at Brussels, dated 1418, and a manu- script has recently been discovered with two plates printed upon it bearing the date of 1406. The history of Alexander, alleged to have been printed from wooden blocks in Italy, in 1284, has been accepted by some authors, and, although it is highly improbable that it was completed at so early a date, it is not impossible, for the reason that only a few years later Marco Polo published a description of Chinese printing, the knowledge of which might have been previously acquired by the mer- chants of Venice in their intercourse with the East. The block-books of the Netherlands are the most important European Specimens of wood-engraving, and they seem to have been printed exactly after the Chinese method. Although the dates of these books cannot be ascertained with accuracy, there is strong confirmatory proof in the fact that one edition of the "Speculum Humarse Salva- tionis," is in the dialect spoken in the Low Countries at the end of the fourteenth century, and the testimony of Ulric Zell upon the use of printed educational and reli- gious books, may be regarded as conclusive. Many of the pictures of these books illustrate the manner of Van Eyck, the leading artist of the Netherlands during the latter portion of the fourteenth century. Many things in these works also exhibit the influence of the customs, tastes, and fashions of the Dukes of Burgundy, whose initials and other insignia appear in the watermarks of the paper. The remarkable originality of ' Flemish art was maintained during the fourteenfh and fifteenth centuries, but an admiration and imitation of the Italian manner became very injurious in the sixteenth century, and continued its influence until, under the great masters, Rembrandt and Rubens, originality and nationality were restored. In Italy, wood-engraving difl, not, as in other countries, precede engraving in metal, and the art im- proved very slowly. The Hypnerotomachis Poliphilii, printed at Venice by Manutius in 1499, contained some wood-cuts of such excellent style that they have been ascribed to the artists Mantegna and Bellini. The ser- mons of Savonarola, published at Florence the day after they were delivered, were illustrated by fine wood-cuts, which afterwards appeared in the "Art of Happy Dying," published in the same city in 1513. The printers of Venice were the foremost patron's of wood engraving in , Italy, and the finest specimens are foiknd in the publica- tions of that city, especially about the year 1550. A history of St. Veronica, published at Milan in 1518, con- ; tains some admirable illustrations.

" Och," said a love-sick Hibernian, " what a recreation tisto be dying in love. It sets the heart aching so delihatelv there's no taking a wink of sleep for the plea- sure of the pain." On a certain clay Jerrold met Mr. Alfred Bunn in Jermyn-street. "What !" said Mr. Bunn, "I suppose you're strolling about, picking up character." " Well, not exactly," was the reply, "though there's plenty lost here. I'm told." "Yes," said a small boy, "when I see a woman run- ning like mad after a tram-car, waving her parasol, and shouting frantically, 'Hi, hi !' I always think that all this trouble might have been prevented if girls were only taught to whistle through their fingers." A nye CUSIATE.-4 Our host," writes a traveller, "was nearly 90 years old, and fond of boasting of Tas- mania's perfect climate, and its conduciveness to longevity. But.' objected one of our party, the ages shown on the tombstones here are not very great; 'That may be,' was the reply- you see, we're a young colony, and the old ones aren't dead yet.'" Mrs. Brougham, mother of the Chancellor, was a. most excellent and thrifty housewife. On one °erasion she was much troubled with a servant addicted to dish- breaking, and who used to allege, in extenuation of her fault, "it was crackit before." One morning little Harry tumbled downstairs, when the fond mother, running after him, exclaimed. "Oh! boy, have you brake your head ?" "No, ma," said the future Chancellor, "it was crackit before." THIS FIGHTING PROCLIVITIES OF latsuwomitte.—How will the learned account, except on the principle of a truly secular heredity, for the fighting proclivities of Irishwomen? Till "The Judgment of Brigh" (697, or thereabouts) women were subject to military duty, fighting in the ranks on exactly the same terms as Hlen. Connected with Adamnan's journey through Ireland at that time, the "annals" record a great event which they dismiss with enigmatical brevity: Dedit degena innocentiuni populis. This event made nothing less than a great social reformation, which was received enthusiastically by the whole people; and the law for exempting women from fighting was called by Adamnan's name. In the " Laebhar Breac " there is the following "Vision of Adamnan," which would be precious if only for its redo- lence of the soil; " Adamnan happening to be travelling one day through the plain of Breg,ia, with his mother on Ms back, when they saw two armies in conflict Then Ronait, mother of Adamnan, observed a woman with a reaping hook in her hand, dragging another woman out of the opposite battalion with the hook fastened in her— for men and women went equally to battle at that time. After this, Ronait sat:down and said: Thou shalt not take me from this spot till thou exemptest women for ever from being in this condition, and from excursions and hostings.' Adamnan then promised that thing," taking advantage of a great religious revival to amelior- ate the condition of Keltic womanhood. Whoever denies the remarkable fighting proclivities of Irishwomen proves himself thereby ignorant of the life of the Irish of our great cities. And yet the compulsory fighting of Irishwomen came to an end 1,200 years ago! Since then women have only fought for pleasure! Was it not O'Connell who overheard this appeal: "Lave go aff me hair, Molly, an' I'll foight tull I doie!" "There isn't a wan in Meath wouldn't carry her round Ireland on his back!" exclaimed an enthusiastic gamekeeper, some years ago, when asked if the people "really liked the Empress of Austria," then in Ireland for a few weeks' hunting; and he had no idea he was using a 1200-year- old locution. And "wouldn't I carry ye, darlint, home on me back, if I could!" was said only last Saturday by a Cerk peasant to the present writer, who hesitated to accept the offer of a lift ins trap.—Getitlensan's How KAVANAGH WON vita VICTORIA CE.066.—0n the 9th of November, when it was known in Lucknow that the army of relief would soon come, Mr. Thoa. Kavanagh, of the uncovenanted service, gallantly volunteered to go forth and make his way to Campbell's camp. It was an enterprise replete with perils, as every outlet was closely guarded by the enemy's posts and pickets, and the way be had top eas lay through the very heart of the hostile city. His object was to give Sir Colin information as to the actual state. of the garrison, and make himself useful as a guide. In going on this duty the brave Irish- man knew well that if he fell into the enemy's hands he would suffer death of the most elaborate cruelty these barbarians could invent. Irehis own narrative he says:— " I was dressed as a budmash. or irregular soldier of the city, with a sword and shield, native-made shoes, tight trousers, a yellow silk koortah over a tight-fitting white muslin shirt, a yellow-coloured chintz sheet thrown round my shoulders, a cream-coloured turban and a white kumurbund. My face down to the shoulders, and my hands to the wrists, were coloured with lampblack, the cork used being dipped in oil to cause the colour to adhere." In this disguise he bade adieu to Outram and his staff, and, provided with a carefully-loaded double- barrelled pistol, set forth under cloud of night, and for- ded the Goomtee, where the water was nearly five feet deep and 100 yards wide. After perils worthy of any ro- mance, he got close to Campbells outposts, and heard the English challenge, " Who'-comes there?" bat with a native accent. "My eyes filled with oyful tears, and I shook the Sikh officer in charge ot the picket heartily b? the hand," he con- tinues. "The old soldier was as pleased as myself when he heard from whence I had come, and he was good enough to send two of his men to conduct me to the camp of the advanced guard. An officer of H.M. 9th Lancers met me on the way and took me to his tent, where I got dry stockings and trousers, and what I much needed, a glass of brandy, a liquor I had not tasted for two months." A flag displayed by Campbell on the summit of Alumbagh, announced to all in the Residency, but chiefly for the information of his wife, that the gal. ant Kavanagh was safe, and had achieved his enterprise, for which he was rewarded by Government with £2,000, admission into the regular Civil Service, and obtained that which he prized more than all—the Victoria Cross. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 2
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 2

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. The directors of the Ship Canal Company have reason to be gratified with the manner in which applications for shares are coming in. During the twenty-four hours which terminated on Thursday forenoon the number of shares applied for was double that of the recent daily average. A meeting, convened by the Mayor of Salford (Mr. Alderman Parmer), at the request of the ratepayers of Pendleton, was held at the Town Hall of...the township on Wednesday night. Mr. Boil:fen' Spencer said that the applications for shares were coming in at the rate of more than .E 50,000 per day. Besides the .E2,1/00,000 already raised there were other sums which they saw in prospect, but which they could not yet, call subscribed capital. In reality about, £700,000 was still wanted, and no ef- fort should be spared tO obtain :this in the next ten days. , Up to the present, time the shares allotted to or applied for by the co-orerative societiesin the Hyde district are about £60,000 in value. At a meeting of the members of the Houghton Green Co-operative Society, recently held, it was decided to take up shares in the Manchester Ship Canal to the value of .£250.

At a special meeting of the members of the Pen- dleton Co-operative Society, it was unanimously decided to take up 400 additional shares in the Manchester Ship Canal, making the total sum now invested by this society £5,000. At 3 meeting of the members of the Bury District Co-operative vision Society, held on Monday evening, it was resolved that the number of shares in the Manchester Ship Canal be increased from 50 to 500, representing, when paid up, £5,000. At a special meeting of the members of the Con- servative Club, St. Stephen-street, Salford, on Wed- nesday evening, Mr. Councilor Robinson in the chair, it was unanimously resolved, on the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. J. Lord, and sup- ported by Mr. J. H. Brown, that shares to the amount of £l,OOO be taken up in the Manchester Ship Canal Company. At a meeting of the Oldham Ship Canal Commit- tee, last night, the Local Secretary reported that, since the commencement, Oldham had subscribed nearly £llO,OOO, of which amount .£35,000 were old applications. The secretary estimated, from pro- mises already made and resolutions passed by limi- ted companies, that the amount in a short time will be raised to £150,000. Stockport is taking up the Ship Canal project in good earnest. On Monday the large model was ex- hibited in the Volunteer Armoury, and was in- spected by thousands of people. The practical result was that over £6,000 worth of shares were taken up in the building, and large promises were made. The local committee have grounds for think- ing that already shares of the value of £lOO,OOO have been taken up in the town and immediate neigh- bourhood.

The Failsworth Limited Companies have looked favourably upon the Ship Canal scheme from the commencement, and at their quarterly meetings, which have just been held, have decided to give further material support to the undertaking. The Ridgefield Spinning Company have resolved to in- vest £l,OOO in the project, the Hope Spinning Com- pany having decided to take 50 additional shares, , which, with the number previously taken, is equiva- lent to £l,OOO, and the Ivy Mill Company also take up 50 .ClO shares. Mr. Ellis Lever writes :—lf every head of a family who can afford it would take one Ship Canal share for each member of the family, the aggregate would reach a considerable sum, and the gift of a share would be a very appropriate Jubilee present. What the value of the shares nay become in a few years I will not venture to predict, but as an illustration of the possibilities of the case I would quote from " Havdn's Dictionary of Dates" a paragraph under the heading of "New River :"—" An artificial river for the supply of London with water, commenced in 1600 and finished in 1613, when the projector, Hugh Myddleton, was knighted by James I. So little was the benefit of it understood that for about 30 years the 72 shares into which it was divided netted only £5 apiece (£360.) Each of these shares was sold originally for .ClOO. Within the last few years they were sold at £9,000 a share, and some lately at £lO,OOO a share." PUBLIC MEETING AT RUNCORN.

Bethesda Lecture:Hall, Runcorn, was crowded on Tuesday evening with an audience gathered to lis- ten to speeches by two representatives of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company Directorate—Messrs Bithel and Crossley. Dr. McDougall occupied the chair, and amongst those present 'were Messrs J. Speakman, W. H. Rogerson, J. H. Salkeld,E.lmison, H. White, S. Taylor, P. Norman, M. Barker, W. Sut- ton, W. Brookes, W. Guest, P. Smith, A. R. Norman, E. Rhodes, T. Cooke, J. Oates, J. Ball, D. Bisbrown, W. G. Cunningham, H. Abrams, F. Beck, R. Eden, J. Sayle, T. Lea, T. Clough, W. 11. Chadwick, Joseph Littler, W. Wright, J. Pickthall, B. Robinson, W. Shaw, T. Capper, J. Picken, G. Yarwood, J.Wil- Hams, W. Hankinson, S. H. Dawson. The Chairman, after describing the steps taken to obtain the Ship Canal Bill, explained that before the first sod was cat the sum of five millions, In addition to the price of the Bridgewater Canal, would have to be raised, and the efforts being made had that end in view. Gentlemen who wished to take shares and encourage an undertaking of this des- cription should do so speedily, as the Act would expire on the 6th August. Questions were iavited before the delegates spoke, and several were handed up. Mr. Bithel undertook the duty of replying. The first inquiry was, what amount the millionaire manufaeturers and merchants, for whose benefit this "bubble scheme" was on foot, had already subscribed? Mr. Bithel said they had already guaranteed towards the three millions which must be raised in Lancashire if they were to get the other five millions in London, the sum of £2,100.000 or £2,200,000. (Applause.) This disposed of the idea that the people of the district looked upon it as a bubble scheme, and they were told that they would easily get the balance In London after Lancashire had shown confidence in the scheme. Another statement was that the canal would take away the bread of the working man by lessening labour. He believed that if this canal was made it would bring snob an amount of prosperity, not only to the working-men of Runcorn, but large numbers of others would earn a very good livelihood. (Hear, hear, and applause.) There was no doubt that all round this district, Runcorn included, they were handicapped for want of cheap access to the sea. If they bad the approach to the port so deepened that the largest vessels in existence could come up to Runcorn with cargoes from all parts of the world, and could take in re- tura their manufactures, instead of the vessels having to be berthed in Liverpool and pay heavy dues, every industry in the district would be stimulated, the value of all property would be raised, and there would be increased employment for every class of people. (Applause.) Mr. Bithel argued that the Staffordshire trade would be exported from Run- corn in preference to Liverpool, which city, he stated, was more prospereua than any' of our manufacturing towns, be. cause she was able to levy such heavy dues upon the raw materials brought into the country, and upon the manu- factured articles leaving it. At one time he was a complete sceptic about the canal, and having had 20 years' experi- ence in the shipping trade and dock management in Melia, he knew something about such matters. He was induced to become a member of a committee to inquire into the, details of the Ship Canal, and after six weeks' close study. he arrived at the conclusion, with 22 other gentlemen, that the canal must be not only of immease benefit to every place on the rents, but that eventually it must be one of the best paying investments that anybody could possibly go in for. (Applause.) With only one-fourth of the trade that went into Liverpool, the canal would pay a handsome divi- dend. He believed that no railway was ever projected that had as good chances of paying, as had this canal. The Bridgewater Canal would at the present time pay al per cent, upon the purchase money, and when it was in the hands Of the company without a single railway man on the Board, they could study the convenience and wants of places like Runcorn, and develops the traffic to make it pay five per cent. (Applause.) The Leeds and Liverpool Canal since it was freed from railway control was paying some- thing like 18 per cent., and shares were at 400 or 500 per cent. premium. After the Ship Canal was made then estuary would remain at their disposal for coasting vessels just as at present, but Runcorn would also be roads into a port available for the largest vessels afloat, and if they would look at the history of any port that had been so im- proved they would find that from that time forth it had got a new lease of life, and enjoyed a prosperity never enjoyed I before. (Applause.) Mr. Crossley then addressed the meeting in support of the scheme. He iaid Mr. Babel's firm had from 15 to 20 thou- sand pounds in the canal scheme. (Applause.) These gentlemen were of the cleverest business men in Manchester and did those present suppose that they would put in that amount of money if they thought it was a bubble. His (Mr. Creasley's) firm had put in 17 thousand pounds, and they did not pretend to be fools at their place. (Applause.) And they did not invest this money for philanthropic rea- sons; they did it because they thought it would Pay- Bs pointed out that the liability of shareholders was limited to the amount of uncalled capital just as it wai limited in rail-- 1 ways. Could our industries live ?against the foreign corni petitition f we did not give them greater facilities of tran- sit? Ile did not think they could. It seemed to him that trade was very rapidly leaving this country. With the long hours worked on the Continent, the little wages paid to men, added t , the fact that they had the best English ma- chinery, and the cheap transit, how could England pretend to keep the markets of the world if we did not increase our facilities. (Applause.) That might not be an argument for investing, but it was a very good argument for making the canal. They wanted to make this canal, and they were going to make it. (Applause.) Mr. C. L. Evans said there was little doubt that if the canal was made Runcorn would be benefitted, and that the working people would be benefitted not only temporarily

II times. He begged to move "That tin :ing late the directors of the Manchester SI Canal •on the prospect of the realisation of tl as impor- sprise. and strongly urges that all the inhabitants of ...uncorn who are in a position to do so not only to take up shares without delay but to exert their influence upon others who may not have. realised personally the com- mercial advantages to be realised from the Manchester Ship Canal as a commercial undertaking; and this meeting pledges itself in that manner to do all in its power to for- ward the object in view." Mr. W. Hankinson seconded the notion. He was sure they would all agree with him that if the canal was a success, which he hoped it would be, it would be a lasting and permanent benefit to the inhabitants of Runcorn. (Ap- planes.) The Chairman, before putting the motion to the meeting, remarked that the greater part of the money spent in con- structing this canal would have to be spent in Runcorn. The canal would be one lake continuous dock from East. ham to Warrington, 21 feet deep, and 121 feet wide; and it would therefore occur to them all that the greater part et the engineering work would be from Old Quay Works to the neighbourhood of Rastham. so that the greater part of the money during construction would naturally be spent In Runcorn. With that prospect, and the prospect that the scheme would revive their drooping industries, it behoved them to encourage the scheme in a substantial manner. (Applause.) The motion was carried unanimously. Mr. J. W. Lightburn, the local agent to the scheme, moved a resolution appointing an executive committee con- sisting of Messrs. Thomas Riley, William Gmest, and Wil- liam Howard, with power to add to their number, carry out the foregoing resolution. Mr. Light- burn made some remarks in favour of the scheme, and said his only interest was tr. develop the trade of the town. So far as his pay was concerned in the official position he held he should be glad to give it up to some public purpose such as baths. (Applause). Mr. W. H. Rogerson seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the chairman the meeting terminated.

div.p: OUR LONDON 'LETTER:

LONDON, TRTIREIDAY. The great event of the Week, obscuring even the interest in the division on the second reading of the Coercion Bill, has been he coup de theeitre of the "Times." What Mr. Wane's uneasy ghost said when it saw the bookstalls flaming with the sensa- tional bill issued from the "Times" office, and on opening the paper discovered a facsimile of a pri- vate letter, is not known:. But after being inces- santly talked over thrott4h four days the almost universal verdict is that the "Times," in its blind and vindictive anger, has got itself into a very nasty place. It will be observed that newspapers ranged I on the same side as that on which the "Times" raves and romps, are cautious not to commit them- selves to any support of the assertion as to the genuiness of the letter which it alleges Mr. Parnell sent to an unnamed correspondent immediately after the Phceuix Park murders. It is the same in Parliamentary circles. Even Lord Randolph Churchill, not accustomed to shirk bold assertion is very cautious in handling the subject. The "Times" itself is getting frightened at its own sudden temerity, and blusters a good deal about other letters of Mr. Parnell which it has in its pos- session. The inference which it is desired Mr. Parnell and the public shall draw from these hints is that there is more matter like the letter put for- ward on Monday, and that it will be well for Mr. Parnell to hesitate before taking action in the mat- ter lest a thunder cloud shoUld burst over and des- troy him. It is quite true that the managers of the "Times" have in their possession some five or six other letters which unquestionably carry the autograph of Mr. Parnell, and are in some cases written in his own hand. But it will hardly be believed, though I I know it as an absolute fact, that these documents are nothing more or less than notes addressed by the leader of the Irish party to the late Mr. Rase, managers of the " Times " Parliamentary corps in the House of Commons. They are mere common places referring to the current business of the House, sometimes in reply to a request for informa- tion from Mr. Ross.

Nothing has as yet been settled with regard to the action to be taken by Mr. Parnell. His denial de- livered in the House of Commons on the eve of the division on the Coercion Bill made a great impres- sion. It was full, comprehensive, and made with manifest sincerity. Usually. a man of icy manner, preserved amid the most turbulent scenes, whilst contradicting the calumny adroitly published with the object of influencing the pending division, Mr. Parnell trembled With emotion, and could scarcely articulate for the burning indgnation that possessed him. No secret is made of the name of the person whom Mr. Parnell suspects of having forged the letter. He was at one time an official of the Land League, but some three or four years ago cut him- self adrift, and has since from time to time occupied himself in making "revelations" which have hither- to fallen very flat. On the stroke of midnight, on Monday last, whilst Mr. Balfour was winding up the debate on the second reading of the Coercion Bill, a curious trans- formation scene came over the Conservative benches. Members returning to their places wore in their buttonhole penny bunches of primroses. They whispered with their neighbours when they took their seats. These stole out of the House, and presently returned each with his penny bunch, till, before Mr. Balfour had brought his dreary harangue to a conclusion, the Conservative benches had blos- somed like the grassy floor of a Kentish wood in primrose time. It was to the foresight of Lord Folkestone that thie early demonstration was due. He had brought down with him after dinner a hamper of bunches of Primroses, and in the earliest moments of Primrose Day had begun their gratui- tous distribution. This was well enough, and so was the show made later in the day, when women, children, clerks, omnibus drivers, and the flunkies on well-appointed carriages sported bunches of the outraged flowers. But it was a different thing with poor Lord Beaconsfield, whose statue in Parliament- square was made the object of a demonstration, well-meant in its intention, but ludicrous in its effect. The base of the statue was piled nearly a foot high with bunches and garlands of primroses, which to-day have become a sickening heap of de- cayet leaves. Worse still, huge coarsely-made gar- lands were cast about the unprotesting head of the hapless statue. These, of the thickness of a ship's life belt six times increased in circumference, were as to the front studded with primroses, whereas the back showed a ghastly expanse of green-glazed calico. There was something intensely life-like in the sardonic look of Disraeli as he peered through this horse collar at the crowd gathered beneath. Desperate and, on the whole, commendable at- tempts were made at the beginning of Mr. W. H. Smith's term of office to represent him as a success. Such an effort is creditable both to the House and Mr. Smith. There is something essentially comical in the notion of Mr. Smith sitting in the seat once filled by Mr. Disraeli and Mr. Gladstone, not to go further back and mention that great statesman to whom Mr. Smith the other day, with quite unusual assumption of superiority, read a lesson in Parlia- mentary Government. but the new leader is a very worthy inoffensive man, who has no enemy unless it be Lord Randolph Churchill, and people like to make things pleasant for him. To this end he contributes a modest manner and retiring dis- position, which imperatively excites sympathy. He effaces himself as much as possihle, and when cir- cumstances drag him to the front he looks so piteously frightened that no one has the heart to make things more uncomfortable for him. Never- theless, the fact remains that Mr. Smith is a mere wooden figure-head, and that just now the House pretty much manages its own affairs with what success the outbreak of Friday night testifies. But though Mr. Smith is not a heaven-born leader of the House of Commons, he is a very I wealthy man, and has an exceedingly satisfactory . notion of a good dinner. Mr. Disraeli, when he was , i

le., 6- - the annual dinner to his sup', on the eve of the session, which pretty fully represen- ted his contribution to the gaiety of the season. Mr. Gladstone entertains more when out of office than when in, and that does not amount to much. His Thursday breakfasts supply his favourite me- dium of dispensinghospitality. Mr. Smith gives:akind of Lord Mayor's dinner nearly every night, at which he feeds in sections his faithful followers Another member of the Ministry has reduced to a system the art of government by dining. This is Earl Onslow, the new Under Secretary of State for the tdlonies., who has really, " sttuck out a new thing. Of course, at Mr. Smith's dinner parties, everything is carried out upon the most approved principles. Dinner dress As de rig- mow, and there is the usual long table with from 16 to 20 guests, an arrangement 'that reduces the gathering to the standard of a table d'hote dinner, where everybody converses ex- clusively with his right or left hand neighbour, and general conversation is impossible. Earl Ons- low has found a better way. His dinner hour is eight o'clock. But if affairs of State prevent any of the guests from arriving 'Punctually it is no matter. There is no big table, but a number of smaller ones set about the room with covers for two, four, and six people. Guests may dress if they please, but they are equally welcome in morning costume. They just drop in, look round the room, and, Seeing a vacant place near a particular ac- quaintance, they occupy it. If they have no choice, they are shown to a table by the Major Porno. This is, of course, the plan, even to the arrangements of the tables, at the first-class hotel restaurants in London and Paris. It is quite new in a private house, and has proved an immense success. The most popular man in the Irish Party at the present moment is not Mr. Parnell, but Mr. Dwyer Gray. Mr. Gray is the proprietor of "Freeman's Journal," which, as everyone knows, was recently bought out as a joint stock company. The concern proved a second Guinness. shares straightway ad- vancing to a premium of seven, that is to say,every allotment of a .£5 share brought to the fortunate holder a present of £7. The number of applica- tions was overwhelming. But Mr. Gray went through them personally, and apportioned his El Dorado with discriminating hand. Every member of the Irish Party had his allotment, varying from 20 to fifty shares. Mr. Parnell, as befitted his high position, received three hundred shares, thee pre- mium on which would be a considerable addition to his fortune. The Irish bishops and priests friendly to the national cause, were not forgotten. lit fact, though the National Party have received from America and elsewhere many windfalls, never was there one like this, in which all classes of workers might participate without qualms of conscience. Mr. Gray, whilst distributing his favours, had the satisfaction of knowing that whilst many made a good thing out of it, none came anywhere near the splendid prize reserved for the fortunate proprietor. A great deal is said and written about the Jubilee being an intolerable subject and the thing being overdone; but I think myself that the London shopkaper knows what he is about, and the Jubilee cry is raised, by him. It is expected that by the end of next month London will be empty of 'Londoners. I was at a house agent's yesterday and was aston- ished at the number of houses that he showed me on his books. It was not what are called "man- sions "—mansions, he explained to me, are London houses with back stair cases—but small houses of .£l5O or I'2oo a year, and above all, flats. It is sup- posed the hotels will be so full that people will be obliged to take flats or lodgings. The same agent told me that an enormous immigration of Ameri- cans lis expected, and that already, by the princi- pal lines, passages are engaged two months in ad- vance.

markably expeditious jerry builder was seen to have run up a tombstone. Indeed, the whole transaction only took about two minutes. The piece was succeeded by a dreadfully solemn farce, in which a Cockneyfied Lan- cashire man, an individual dressed in a suit of rusty black, and supposed to be a doctor, an umbrella of ab- normal dimensions, and an idiotic head, which would persist in appearing on the stage without any visible means of support, are inextricably mixed together in my mind. You can take your choice of the other shows. On the one hand there is a circus on such an exceedingly small scale that the horses accustomed to racing round the ring therein woulda verily believe, be capable of per- forming their cuatomary evolutions on the rim of a "Jim crow" hat. On the other an exceedingly large horse is on view.. I have Been the animal outside, swathed in woollen shawls, and from the manner in which he throws out his forelegs I should say that in a previous state of existence he had a very intimate ac- quaintance with the prize ring. I must not forget to mention also a young lady, in another show, blessed, ac- cording to the illustration outside, with a very preposes- sing appearance and cursed with an insatiable appetite for such indigestible articles as long knives and swords. Her interior by this time must be very much like a cullender. I mourn the absence, however, of such old friends of my youth as the spotted and fat ladies, the giant, the dwarf, the performing pig, and the oyster that could whistle a tune. In my grief Ispend money recklessly on the emasculated pleasures of ball throwing, pile driving, and weight pulling, with an occasional ride on the hobby horses and the dry land sailing ships, which makes me heartily sick; winding up the evening with an indis- criminate supper of hot peas, black puddings, and ice cream, the natural consequence being that my dreams during the night will not soon be forgotten. Methought, as I lay in bed, that the gigantic horse stood on his hind legs on my chest, and Mr. Bailey, by pulling at his tail, I made him gyrate his forefeet in a manner seriously threatening the symmetry of my features. Close by stood the Mexican with a knife in his hand, with which he proposed to demonstrate to the fair lady at his side that it was possible to send it through my heart without injuring me. My cries for assistance were utterly drowned by the steam organ, grinding out the latest popular air. The Showman, who saw my agony, pointed I derisively to a ghostly-looking tombstone, on which was inscribed my name and age, and a legend to the effect that, though a good Christian and an estimable father, I fell a victim to an inordinate love for Easter Fairs.

A NIGHT AT A LANCASHIRE FAIR.
(By A. Gomm.)

I don't intend giving you a guide book description of the scene, or to catalogue the amusements as an auc- tioneer would do, but simply to dot down a few things which may be seen in the astonishing salmagundi of tag-rag and. bobtailism which at present crowds the Market Ground almost to the entire strangulation of the I traffic. Step this way. In front of you is a painting in oils which does more credit to the artist's imagination than to his accuracy. It depicts an ourang-outang- looking being covered with hair, and visitors are invited to step inside and view the strange creature at the small cost of one penny. This is what occurs inside. Show- man comes up with a stick, raps the top of a large box —in which, presumably, the sea serpent is stowed safely away until he has finished digesting his last meal of old rope—and calls out, "Hie, hie!" Movement behind a dirty curtain in the corner and appearance-therefrom of an ancient "pepper-and-salt" Dobbin, own brother to Don Quixote's famous steed. There's a strong family likeness between the two in the face, for both rejoice in the " Romanist " of noses. Elsewhere, the resemblance is not quite so marked, for Dobbin of the show appears in all the glory of striped head, legs, and barrel. The showman informs the astonished public that the animal before them is something between a donkey and a zebra, and is known in natural history as a quagga. Dobbin flicks his ears at this point as if to resent the imputation that he is anything of the sort, and one irate spectator declares derisively that the ani- mal is a cross between a hippopotamus and a giraffe, and wants to bet the showman "five bob" that a brush and a bucket of soap and water will prove the quagga a fraud. Just when the conversation is becoming interest- ing and promising to lead to the showman's head being punched, that astute individual sends Dobbin back again into obscurity, and trots up the terrible creature in hair. There steps on to the boards, in reply to a signal, a very ordinary individual, who certainly does rejoice in more than the usual hirsute endowment. The showman grati- fies the audience with the solemn information that the individual before them is a Christian—all the more as- tonishing, it would appear,from the fact that he is half a negro and half a white man. One of the audience hazards the suggestion that he was born at Cork, that his father knew something of a certain pig which "paid the rint," and that his mother's name was Kathleen Mavourneen. The rest of the audience laugh, and the showman joins them and announces that all is over. Across the way an entertainment widely different claims attention. A middle sized individual, with long -lank hair, and a cast of features which suggest that he is a Mexican, stalks about a raised platform, attired in ' Garibaldi shirt, white leather trousers, and high boots. A round soft hat on his head and a revolve(r case at his belt completes his costume. Two or three other men in Garihaldian attire walk about, and a female occasionally putnin an appearance. This lady's dress is most bizarre. It resembles nothing in the world so much as that of a Spanish bull fighter; and the occupation she follows appears every whit as dangerous as that of the Matador, whose costume she affects. Inside the tent before which these people parade is a platform about two feet high. at one extremity of which stands the Mexican, and at the other the female above referred to with a potato in her hand. The Mexican fires a shot from a gun at the potato and shatters it into a thousand atoms. A similar performance takes place with the potato on her head, the Mexican, by way of variation discharging his gun over his head and between his legs. H then outlines her figure on a board by throwing at her a number of sharp knives, which stick with their points in the wood close to her dress. The second act in this horrifying drama—which may some day prove to be a tragedy—is brought to a close by the Mexican throwing a knife across the woman's throat, while she stretches her head well back. He lastly repeats the knife-throwing per- formance, but substitutes gigantic axes for daggers. The performance appeals to the morbid tone of sensation, and one can't help watching it with feelings somewhat akin to those of the gentleman of independent means , who spent his time and his substance in travelling from town to town with a menagerie of wild beasts in the hope some day of seeing the performing lions worry their keeper. No sooner are we outside the tent again than a little gentleman in a dress suit, with a shiny hat and an amazing wealth of shirt front, makes an irresistible appeal to patronise his ghosts. For the small considera- tion of 2d. we find ourselves admitted to the front seats, with plenty of time before us to admire the gorgeous creatures who are constantly paying flying visits to the green room, the said green room apparently con- sisting of a small recess in the front of a van, curtained off from the vulgar gaze. What do these temporary visits mean ? The leading lady it struck me, utilised the fleeting moments at her dis- posal by getting tip a mildilirtation with the demoniacal being who played such a prominent part in the subse- procmga, and the quentleading gentleman, like a barrister, possibly required constant "refreshers." The young lady, who I presume does the understudy for the leading part, took my eye the most. Her dorsal ex- pansion was something tremendous. The ingenious arrangement of bent wire hoops and striped calico she , wore was the evident envy of her sex. One member of ' the company—a tall, powerful creature, clad in a coat of tin mail; with aihelinet on his head, and red tights— was so lost in his admiration of her that he stumbled against her, and she gave him a push which sent him staggering. The little lady had evidently a will of her own, notwithstanding her sweet looks. The curtain rises at this point, and everybody's attention is centred on the play. A gentleman,with a very spikey moustache and a costume which seems a cross between a pantaloon and Mephistopheles, explains that the scene about„to be enacted is the death of a soldier's child. I confess that ; the performance rather shocked me, for the sad scene was hurried through in such indecent haste. The breath was no sooner out of the child's body than some re-

towd wi should aft go aw raandbi Liverpoo' flirtet gig to it. Well! wi powlert on past Garston, mills, an Knott's Hole, wheer tin sed ther WUS bottom, an a bad place furt anchor, o' astham bank, an' so across th' E river to Broul„. Do. opposit th' candle works. Here wi leet go_vaL r ker, an teed th' sails up, Ah ! it vtur like mwsr:,,ht, heaven! Aw so quiet an' still after th' rel!rtii; an Jouterin wid ad ate i' th' broad ocean middle o' th' river. Wen things wur straightened up a bit, agra onr, began =akin' kettle-wedges an' fire-stick bon , an mackin a fire. Th' kettle war aeon bilin raan o.enn flsin late it grond stile. Wile wid bin watein this th chap ad bin luggin' sate ther grub a/Iff' ragnsl far th' tas. One fella wur screwin' th yeds °— roast. herrin an' stickin um under th grate furt wur Wen th' water wur temt upo' th' taa, 411' ger aw Beet daan weer wi could find a place-4 ewint, we th' loaves an fishes spread aw abate, Wisforere happy, an' tho'wid fargetten fur say grace begun, wi did better tin that, wid a thaak spent aw th' time wi wur eightin •
RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.

A GLAD FIRESIDE. Workin' fooak, as a rule, ged smo' pleashurt Except wod they mek for thersels; • An' it's sweeter to fill one's own meashur, , Than to trust fort to somebody else. . Wheer comfort is, joy's somewheere lurkin r To flash t' lest o' mirth clear on't' face , Un when a chap's fagged eawt wi' workin True pleashur's but fun i' one place ! That's wheer t' wife an' t' kettles booath sub— Wheer th' child wants a cock-hoss to ride: , An' t' jcpyllells o'th' heart start o' ringin't Luv's jingles bi th' hooam fireside! This life's dark or lest—as yo' mek It's not th' world, but fooak ut's to blame.,, If go've th' chance to enjoy yotsel'—teli " An' begrudge nobry else as does t' same. Do yo'r nook, fur un squr, at yo'r labour, Un be civil an' kind i' yo'r speech, Dornd " nag" nor fo eawt wi' yo'r naybsri Then yo'r rest way o' livin, ull teych As th' sunshinenshine o' life's th' hearts own rse Un as Honesty's nowt mitch to hide • Then at th' same time they'll see Virtue d Yor blossoms bi th' glad fireside! Its ronk folly to chunner an' grumble Bekose somebry's heigher nor yo. Gradely fooak uts contented, tho' humble, Know weel as they'n nod fur to fe Pride, at times, o' wax wings does a flutter Un flashes abeawt paycock-gay, Then id drops wi' a flop into th' gutter ,-- Every foe, like a deg, has id day! But ther's surnmat mooar lovely an' iastid, Than t' pomp an' fine fithers e' Pride ; • That's th' glow o' true hearts, breetly Ther gleeams reawnd a calm fireside. What's th' use ov a soarise ambition! When th' wings are too wayk to uprise? Reflect, an' yo'll find yo've a mission,-:Ji - Though Tor lowly, yor lot dorn'd despise ! Dorn'd pine after wod yo' con never God up to; it's folly to fret; But i' yo'r own sphere mek endeavour To gee eawt o' misery's net. Away wi' yo'r dea,wts, send o' fear hence/ Yo'r' but one an' th' world's big an' wide; Press on! wi' rest good perseverance— Faith comes to a glad fireside!

Wod sufferin', wod trials an' danger. Ther is for o th' wanderers as rooam Forrun lands—rest to them is a stranger-7.m f They've left wod they. want mooast at hooi*-- If it's sum gowden gain as they're seekire!Ag. Hooam's th' place for't feawnduhitn o' Theer thrift a start soon could be rnekkiri Beawt drivin' off pleashur an 'ealth: It's th' best place o sooarts o' weather To shelter—wode'er may betide— An' wheer true hearts poo cheerful together' Life's glory's at th' hooarn fireside! The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. Bius Anystmzo.—The Merchant Shipping (Inshing Boats) Bill and the Isle of Man Customs Bill passed through Committee.—The Army (Annual) Bill was read a third time and passed. THE IRISH JUDICATURE.—IMPORTANT CHANGES. The Earl of CADOGAN moved the second reading of the Supreme Court of Judicature (Ireland) Bill, and ex- plamed that it had been rendered necessary by the vacancy in the Chief Justiceship of the Common Pleas in Ireland by the elevation of Chief Justice Morris, and Its object was to avoid filling up the vacancy. It pro- vided for the abolition of the offices of Chief Justice of the Common Pleas and Chief Justice of the Exchequer, filling up the vacancies of those offices by appointing puisne judges, and assimilating the arrangement to that now, adopted in the English Courts by merging the Com- mon Pleas and Exchequer into the Queen's Bench Divi- sion.

Lord DENtrAN moved that the bill should be read a second time that day six months, on the ground that its object was to put an end to a system which had always worked well. Lord FITZGERALD approved of the consolidation of the three divisions of the High Court in Ireland. The bill was right in principle, and he hoped the amendment would not be persevered with. • Earl SPENCER considered the question of law reform in Ireland a very important one, and a field in which the Government might do a large and useful work. As faT as he understood the bill, it met with hisrentire appro- val, though he should have been glad if it had gone further in the direction of the bill of 1885. Lord DENMAN withdrew his amendment, and the bill was read a second time. COURSE or Busurivzs.—ln reply to Earl Spencer, the Earl of CADoomr stated that it was his intention to ask the House to read the Irish Land Law Bill a second time on Thursday next —Lord Bit/pommy, supposed it would not be proposed to take the report stage of the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill on the same evening.— Lord STANLEY of PRESTON replied that he thought TUEs. day next would be a convenient day for taking that report. • The House adjourned at 4 65 p.m.

POLICE ENFRANCHISRMENT.--Mr. BURDETT DOUTTS, in moving the eecond reading of the Police Force Entrench's- talent Bill, said that it did not extend to the police of Ire- land, but it was identical with other police enfranchisement bills that had been introduced into that house.—Mr. T. W. liussuLL hoped that the Government would not consent to inflict any civil disability on the Irish police.—The HOME SIICEIRTARY said be had not given the pledge asked, because he did not know the opinion of the Government on the matter, but he thought he could promise the Irish members that its provisions would not be extended. to Ireland.— The bill was afterwards read a second time without a division. SCOTCN LAND TINLIRE.—Mr. BARCLAY moved the second reading of the Land Tenure (Scotland) Bill. A long dis- cussion followed.—The LORD ADVOCATE contended that there was no analogy between the condition of farm tenants in Scotland and in Ireland, and went on to show that the bill contained provisions as to rents which in former years the tenants objected to. He orpoeed the COCH• RARE BAILLIR also opposed it, and was speaking against it when the debate stood adjourned. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tn-unsass. - -

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. There was a tolerably full house, aid several peeresses occupied seats in the side galleries. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—Earl CADOGAN moved the second reading of the Irish Land Law Bill, and Lord DENMAN moved that it be read a second time that day three months, his principal objection being its tendency to make the State the great proprietor of land in Ireland.—Earl SPENCER sup- portedithe second reading, saying that without a settlement of the land question they could not expect to have peace or order in Ireland—Lard CARNARVON supported the measure, as did also Lord Fitzgerald and Lord Ashbourne.—On the motion et the Doke of ARGYLL, the debate was ad- journed. BILLS READ A THIRD TIME.—The County Courts (Ex- penses) Bill, the Merchant Shipping (Fishinz Boats) Bill, and the Isle of Man (Customs) Bill were read a third time and passed. . o'clock. HOUSE OP COMMONS.—Tnuasosy. . .

Golan, replying to Mr. Baden- Powell, said in the present state of Indian finances it was impossible to entertain the idea of repealing the duty on rice.—Questions were answered respecting the Suakim- Berber railway plant, the Ruby Mines in Burmah, Welsh intermediateNeducation, and the latest Ordnance scandal, Mr. Stanhope, in regard to the fatter subject, confirming the reported discharge of an official for a grave breach of trust, —Mr. sexton elicited from the Speaker that suspended members were allowed to sit in the Strangers' Gallery, and that no distinction was made in the case of Mr. Healey.— Mr. Dillon obtained leave to make a personal explanation, and denied the recent assertion of Lord Hartington that two men who bad acted for months under his (Mr. Dillon's) directions went about Ireland counselling assassination.

ACCIDENT.—RE-TXTERMENT OF PRESI- DENT LINCOLN. NEW YORK, SATURDAY.—A violent cyclone has passed ever Belmont county, Ohio. Thirty persons were injured and great damage was done to property. . PHILADELPHIA, MONDAY—TWO goods trains collided at Palatine, Illinois, on Sunday, attracting a crowd or spectators, near a large water tank, which Suddenly burst, deluging the crowu,,killing six, fatally injuring four, and seriously injuring others. The shock of the collision is believed to have loosened the tank hoops. The remains of President Lincoln, says a telegram from New York, have been removed from the secret grave In which they were deposited at Springfield, Illinois, and have been reburied with those of his wife in the same cemetery. The object of the secret burial was to pre- vent the body being stolen, and the exact spot was for several years known only to a few persons. A reek slide has occurred near Ruenavista, Colorado, by which eight persons were killed and several others injured. THE CROWN PRINCE OF GERMANY. Bastin, WEDNESDAY.—There is no foundation for the statement made in a communication published yesterday by the "Temp.," from its Berlin correspondent, asserting that the Crown Prince was attacked by cancer of the throat. The malady from which his Imperial Highness is suffering is chronic catarrh of the throat.

MORE PLOTS AGAINST THE CZAR. VIENNA, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—In Kief and Odessa the police have lately made discoveries which show that the Nihilists had laid plots to assassinate the Czar when he visited those cities. In Kief the railway was under- mined over which the Imperial train would pass, while in Odessa the railway station was to have been blown up.

TEIE BUDGET.

At seven minutes past five Mr. GoscHme rose to introduce his Budget. lie estimated the surplus for the coming year at £974.000, which he proposed to increase to the extent of £lOO,OOO by raising the present stamp duty of 2s 6d per cent on debenture stock to 10s, and patting such stock on the same footing as ordinary and preference stock. He pro- posed to reduce the amount paid for interest on the National Debt to £26,000,000 and take a penny off the income tax. Tobacco duties he proposed to reduce from 3s 6d to 3s 2d per pound, and there would be a slight change in the stamp duty of marine policies. Farmers will also have the option of paying income tax on their net profits instead of half their rent. Sir W. HARCOURT asked what the Chancellor of the Exchequer intended to do with the gold coinage, which was a disgrace to the country, and adversely criticised the proposal to abandon the provision for the payment of the National Debt, which, he said, was the greatest encouragement any Finance Minister could give to reckless and extravagant expenditure —Lord R. CHURCHILL remarked that the Bud- , get showed how great was the value of a reputation, for if he (Lord R. Churchill) had made such proposals he would , have roused the indignation of every person in the country who thoeght himself a financier. He regretted that the Chancellor of the Exchequer had not said one real word on the subject of economy and retrenchment, but he had in- jured the cause by his proposals. He hoped the House would net encourage the Chancellor of the Exchequer in a system of unsound finance which must lead to extravagance and bar the way to any retrenchment. Of the two he pre- ferred the Budget of Sir W. Harcourt last yin to that of Mr. Goschen this year.—Mr. GOSCHEN, answering his critics at a late hour, took these rebukes good-naturedly, and I assured the noble lord that the Budget really was all his own.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, in avower to a question by Sir W. Harcourt, said if it would be for the convenience of the House, the debate on the Budget would be resumed on Mon- day.—After some remarks by Colonel Blundell, the first resolution, relating to tobacco duties, was finally agreed to, and the House resumed. The Criminal Law (Scotland) Procedure Bill was read a second time.—The Metropolitan Open Spaces Aets Exten- sion Bill, as amended, was considered. Tbe House adjourned at a quarter to two o'clock.

THE rEKENIX -PARK -MURDIRS AND MR. PARNELL.—A GRATE CHARGE. I Monday's Times concluded a series of articles 'on "ParnelEsm and Crime," We (said The Smos) inti- mated that, besides the damning. facts which we there recorded, unpublished evidence existed which would bind still closer the links between the "constitutional" chiefs and the contrivere of murder and outrage. In view of the unblushing denials of Mr. Sexton anellfr. Healy on Friday night, we do not think it right to withhold any longer from public knowledge the fact that we possess, and have had in our custody for-some time, documentary evidence which has, a most serious bearing on the Parnellite conspiracv, and which, after a most careful and minute scrutiny, is, we are satisfied, quite authentic. We produce one document in fac- simile to-day by a process the accuracy of which cannot be impugned, and we invite Mr. Parnell to explain how his signature has become attached to such a letter. It is requisite to point out that the body of the manuscript is apparently not in Mr. Parnell's hand- writing, but the signature and the "Yours very truly" unquestionably are so; and if any member of Parlia- ment doubts the fact, he can easily satisfy himself on the matter by comparing the handwriting with that of Mr. Parnell in the book containing the signatures of members when they first take their seats in the Hons. of Commons. The body of the letter occupies the whole of the first page of an ordinary sheet of stout white notepaper, leaving no room in the same page for the signature, which is placed on the fourth page near the top right- hand corner. It was an obvious precaution to sign upon the back instead of upon the second page, so that the half-sheet might if necessary be torn off and the letter disclaimed. It is right and neciposary to explain that the "Dear Sir" is believed to be Egan, and that the letter was addressed to him in order to pacify the wrath of his subordinate instruments in the Phmnix Park murders —then (on May 15, nine days after the tragedy) still at large and undetecte44 The anxiety of the writer to keep his address unknown will be noted, and is curious in connection with a belief prevailing at the time that Mr. Parnell was so impressed by the danger he had in- curred by denouncing the ammssinations as to have applied for the protection of the police on the plea that his life was in peril. In the facsimile which we place before our readers the paper lies open, the first page being to the right, and the fourth to the left. 15/5/82. DEAR 'SIR, I am not surprised at your friend's anger, but he and you should know that to denounce the murders was the only course open to us. To do that promptly was plainly 14ie-only-cour our best policy. But you can tell him and all others concerned that though I regret the accident of Lord Y.Cavendish's death I cannot refuse to admit that Burke got no more than his deserts.

You are at liberty *o show him this, and others whom you can trust also ; jmt, let not my a.ddraes be known. Be can write to Rouge of Commons. Yours very truly, CHAS. S. PARNELL. ABSOLUTE DISAVOWAL BY MR. PARNELL.

Mr. Parnell declares that the letter attributed to him by The Times is nothing more nor less than oeclumsy forgery. The handwriting, he says, in no way resembles that of any'person who ever acted as his amanuensis, whilst the signature is a bad imitation. He fancies he sees in the handwriting a resemblance to that of a person with whom he was in correspondence about eighteen months ago, and his present suspicion is that the body of the epistle and the signature are the work of one hand. The hon. member has telegraphed for letters which he received from the individual in question, and if his sus- picion be confirmed after a close scrutiny, he will take steps to bring the alleged fraud home to the perpetrator. He does not conceal his opinion that the person whom he suspects is sufficiently unprincipled to commit a fraud of the kind suggested. Mr. Parnell admits that at the first cursory glance the alleged fac simile bears a general resemblance to his signature. Indeed, before making a close exeraination he assumed, knowing that the text of the document was never dictated by..hira, either that an autograph given by him to some political admirer had been utilised by the forger, or that the per- son responsible for the document had somehowobtaihed possession of -sheet of notepaper on which he had written his name for his secretary's use. In the first coanection Mr. Parnell explains that it is no uncommon thing for him, when asked for his autograph, to place it 'lige of notepaper. It will be noted that ia nt the the toletpMorf a alleged to have emanated from Mr. Parnell the signature is placed at. the top of the page, and the writing on the first page lecrowded towards the bottom, as though the 'denature had been previously filled in. Mr. Parnell states that frequently, when in a hurry, he ~ has left a sheet or two of notepaper, signed, for his secretary cretay to All in the body of the letters at his leisure. On closer iasPeetion of the alleged fac-simile, however, Mr: Parnell discards this theory altogether, and emphati- cally declares that the signature is a forgery, calling attention to several important differences which would immediately strike an expert in handwriting. Mr. pencil points out several other details in which his in- eieiduality has not been faithfully copied, and in preof at his allegations• produced a large bundle of cheques bearing his signature, and invited comparison. In May, 1882, when the incriminating letter is alleged to have been written, Mr. Henry Campbell, now a member of Parliament, was Mr.,Parnell's private secretary. On . Monday a reporter had an interview -with Mr. Parnell on the subject of the letter. Mr. Parnellpointed out that.although at first sight some of the letteeein the signature attached to the farsivrile letter appeared to resemble those in his autograph, on close comparison there is a decided and striking difference in many im- portant points. For example, Mr. Parnell's signature invariably stapes in an upward direction, whereas the signature in The IVzses slopes downwards. Again, Mr. Parnell in signing his name place.s a fullpoint after the "S," while in The Times signature no such stop appears. Mr. Parnell further pointed out that the "r" in "Parnell" and the " C " in "Charles" are quite different from any- thing he has written. The "Cli" in "Charles" are of abnormal length, very much longer, Mr. Parnell asserts, than he has ever written them. With regard to the signature generally, the hon. gentleman stated that it is in the handwriting of a person accustomed to writing a flowing hand, while his own handwriting is cramped in style. The letter and signature Mr. Parnell characterised as impudent forgeries, and he stated that he has a streng suspicion as to the identity of the writer. Mr: H. Labouchere, M.P., writes to the Daily News.— With regard to the charge made by Colonel Saundereon against the Irish Nationalist members, and the alleged letter of Mr. Parnell which was published in The Tunes, I beg to enclose the accompanying telegram that I have received from Mr. Patrick Egan :—"Saunderson'S state- ment that I presided at a supper in celebration of the Phenix Park murders is a wilful slander. I never even heard of such a celebration. Mr. Parnell never wrote me any such letter as that quoted in The Tinges. The whole thing is a base fabrication." Commenting upon the latest phases of the Parneß tool- U'S Echo (Unionist Liberal) says the runes has ft"the world the fac simile of a forged letter. It is the Ti.Xle3 to prove that th• original is gesanin. e. It has not even attempted to prove it., and tmless the Mines is prepared to give more evidence than it has published, it has made* mistake, and weakened many of itn recent ukterances.

IRELAND.
The newly-formed company for exporting Irish manu- factures has purchased a first consignment of Blarney Tweeds.

Two childreNt-wins, aged about Ave years, were run over and killed by the limited mail train near Castlebar, on Saturday. The parents, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Chan- ning, of Ballyyary-, were at the time attending market in Castlehar.

James APLoughlan, master of the schooner Thomas Pearson, was charged, at Cork, on Saturday, with shoot- ing at and killing Daniel Malcahn an army reserve man. There had been a di-', between the parties. These- bused, who denied the setence. was committed for trial. The Rev. testthew Macaulay, Presbyterian minister of Kelveys Gruel, Castlehlany, wrote to the Freesias', Journal, on Sate-4day, that he has been ruthlessly boy- cotted for professine Gladstenian principles. Fifty, families of his congivg.tion refuse to pay his stipend: his wife and himself have been assaulted; and he has re- signed the pastorate. A man named Burkett was killed on Sunday near KM- °TOM, county Kerry. A dispute occurred detween him and a neighbouring farmer named Shea in reference to the grazing of a piece of land. Burkett found a number of Sheets cattle on the land, and he proceeded with some men to turn them off. Shea with his friends resisted, and attacked Burkett and his party. A severe encounter followed, in the course of which sticks and stones were used, anti Burkett was struck on the head with a spade handle:causing fatal injuries. Five arrests have been made. REVOLT OF HUSH PuLiCEMEN AGAINST THE COERCION BILL. Seven constables of the Royal Irish Constabulary tendered their resignation, Monday, with the following letter to the Inspector-General. Numerous resignations are expected to follow :—" We, the undersigned members of the Royal Irish Constabulary, find ourselves com- pelled to tender you our resignation, and to sever our connection with the force. For the years that we hate been in the force we carried out faithfully the very irksome and odious duties which our position and discipline imposed on us, even though ' free qnently we were thus brought into collision with the people, and felt that we were made the instruments of inflicting upon them grievous wrong. Our own bitter experience in early life could leave us in no doubt as to the burning grievances under which the farming riasses in this country suffer, and we feel cer- tain that you will 'readily recognise. We speak the feeling of a large body in the police force when wo say that it was by no small effort we succeeded, in-obedience to our oath and our duty, in repressing-theSfeefings with which we found ourselves obliged to look on, and even assist in, evictions we well knew to be cruel and unjust. Our position, unpleasant and hateful as it has been in the past, would, we believe, be rendered unendurable by the proposals of the new Coercion Bill, which would make us the instruments of entirely suppressing the liberties of our fellow countrymen and our priests-- (Signed) William Fttxpatrick, constable, 7 years' services Denis Hanley, constable, 5 years'..service; Thomas Fal- lon, constable, 5 years' service; James IPNalty, con- stable, 6 years' service; Edward Coghlan,. constable, 5 ' years' service; John O'Rourke, constable, 7i ,years' ser- vice; Manus Friel, constable, 3 years' service.' Much excitement prevailed at Castlelsland, on Monday- eight, a torchlight procession parading the town, singing a God Save Ireland." On reaching the Crown Hotel, the crowd cheered the seven constables who had resigned, and Mr. Fitzpatrick, one of the men, explained the reason of their resigning, which he said was perfectly free from any stigma that would disgrace them. They declined to fellow the bailiff, or seize cattle. He asked for cheers for Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Dillon.

I'MArlstaans IN LENT AND MAY.—From Ash Wednesday to Easter Eve there were only recorded in the Miles 127 land, solemnised in the Anglican churches in Eng. , and, Wales, and Ireland. Scotch marriages are not in- cluded, but they were very few, nor those solemnised abroad, but recorded in Lent, though solemnised pre- iviously. On four days there were no such marriages; and on three only one. A great number were chronicled in Easter week, and during the next fortnight there will 'be very many weddings, as there is a strange prejudice against marriages in May. THE GREEK GIPSIES rx LOKDON.—The Greek gipsies , left Durham at eight o'clock on Saturday morning for London, where they arrived shortly after two in the afternoon. There were six women, five men, three girls, and twelve boys, some being babies in arms. They are in a deplorable and ill-clad condition, and appeared to be suffering severely from cold. No arrangements appear to have been made for them upon their arrival, and the authorities seemed at first perplexed .as to what should be done with them. Although suffering from insufficient clothing, the nomads appeared to be amply provided with focd, but for some time they huddled themselves together on the platform, piteously inquiring for ground upon which to erect tents. Superintendent Parish and Mr. Vizier, in order to make the best arrange- ments possible, suaveyed the station, and ultimately decided to place them in a covered-in portion of the York-road Stationyard, pending arrangements as to their next destination.

WIIOLES*LE POTATO FRAUDS.—On Saturday a man, who described himself as William Edgeley, wholesale fruit and potato merchant, Smithfield Market, was brought up at Macclesfield, charged with fraud. It was stated that the prisoner, on the 21st March, called on the prosecutor, a farmer at North Rode, and, representing that he was a potato merchant in a large way of busi- ness, bought from him 35i loads of potatoes at 6s. 9d. per load, prisoner to pay the carriage and reniit by cheque on delivery. The order was completed in a few days, but prosecutor heard no more of Edgeley. Pro- ceeding to Smithfield Market, he found that prisoner was not a stall-holder there, and he could Team nothing ' except that the potatoes had been delivered to prisoner. I who paid the carriage, and then sold them to various persons at 6s. per load. A warrant for Edgeley's appre- bes 'sion was placed in the hands of Police Constable !Cayes, whe found his man in Manchester.—On this 1 evidence the prisoner was remanded. EXECUTION OE THE HOXTON ItII7RDEILEIL—CONFICSSION. —The convict Carrell, found guilty of the murder of Lydia Green, his sweettkert, in Ffoxton, was hanged in Newgate Gaol, on Monday morning, at 8 o'clock. The prisoner, from the time of his arrest down to the last moment, appeared perfectly unconcerned, and troubled himself very little with what was going on around him. He spoke but little in the condemned cell, and outwardly showed no remorse for the terrible and utterly motive- less crime of which he had been convicted. His rela- tives visited him once or twice, and the interviews on-those occasions were very affecting; but after their departure the convict soon relapsed hato his callous mood. To the minister who had sought to give him spiritual consolation in his hour of need, Cerrell had admitted his guilt, but declared that he had no knowledge of what he was doing at the time. Neither did he give the slightest indication of the motive which led him to slay the poor girl who had so implicitly trusted him. Unmet' learned on Satqrday night that there was not the slightest prospect of a reprieve being granted, and there- upon resigned himself to his fate. He maintained his usual composure throughout Sunday, employing his hist day upon earth in writing several letters. He retired to rest at an early hour in the evening, and appeared to sleep well. He stood upon the scaffold with his eyes closed, taking no interest in what was going on around him, looking pale and haggard in the gray morning light. He spoke no word as Berry deftly bound his legs, nor made any response to the chaptaia's prayers. Directly the signal was given, Berry pulled the lever, the drop gave way, and the wretched convict disappeared from view. A slight vibration of the cord ensued, but the officials of the gaol declared that death was instantaneous. On Sunday Correll also applied himself in writing a full confession of the crime of which he was convicted. It has been forwarded by the Governor (Col. Milman) to the Horne Se,xctary. In this confession the culprit admitted the justice of his sentence, and declared the murder was premeditated, and actuated by jealousy. He purchased the revolver very shortly before, and paid Is. ad, for it. There was no quarrel between the deceased and himself, sad he fired the pistol at her without a word being uttered. After the crime he proceeded as fast as he could to the residence of his father, and. on his way he thzesar Ow weapon over one of the canal bridges. A NOTABLE PICTERE.—A recent Paris letter to a London paper contains a graphic description of Mr. Henry Mosler's latest painting, which is just now receiving the finishing touch at his studio in the Rue de la Tr6mouille. This picture illustrates a pathetic incident in the life of the North American Indians, and is the largest picture Mr. Mosier has yet painted. The picture is the first one of a series of three which Mr. Mosier has undertaken to paint for Mr. H. H. Warner, of Rochester, New York, U.S.A., a well-known patron of the arts and sciences, and who has gained a world- wide reputation by reason of his celebrated Warner's Safe Cure, which has been marvellously successful in the treat- ment of diseases of the kidneys and liver, which bad hereto- fore been considered by the medical profession as incurable. It is stated the price for the three pictures is to be £60,000. The studies were made lay Mr. Mosier during his recent visit to the United States, where he spent several weeks among the Apache Indians of Arizona.
