She jumped out, falling on her head, and was conveved home in an unconscious state. St, •ontinued in th-at. condition un • •r(l On Monday a child named Joseph Moran, eon of a. labourer, living in HaElwell-road, Bolton, died, it is sup-, posed, from illness attributable to vaccination. Prior to vaccination the child had perfect health, but immedi% ately afterwards became ill. After the customary removal of the matter the infant grew rapidly worse and died in convulsions. An inquest will be held. At Manchester, on Monday, T. Morris, an elderly man, was charged with obtaining £5O by false pretences, and also with misappropriating £4,000 belonging to the Bridgewater Loan Society, for which he anted as agent for many years. The prisoner, who denied that there had been any fraud whatever, was remanded, and the magistrates offered to take bail for his appearance. The Bolton Coroner inquired on Monday into the suicide of an outdoor labourer named Thomas Ir!ern, 58 years of age, of Lever-street, Bolton. Irlam had been out of work nearly all the year, and was consequently very depressed in spirits. He complained bitterly that there were now "so many young 'uns that there was no chance for the old 'uns." A verdict of suicide whilst of unsound mind was returned." TF.RRIBLE SUICIDE.—A man. aged about 56, died on Monday morning at Sheffield Hospital from terrible injuries mused by jumping from the fifth storey window of a lodging-house on Sunday night. The porter saw him about to jump, and rushed to save him, but wastoo late. He fell SO feet, and was fearfully mangled. He was in great poverty. His name is supposed to be William Makepeace. He had letters with the Liverpool postmark. THE ASSASSINATION Or COF.ONEL RODEN.—The body of the late Colonel Roden, commanding officer of the South Wales Borderers Volunteer Babtalion, who was barbar- ously murdered at the lead mine at Caloi in Corsica on March 15th, arrived at Tyrhituusk, his Welsh residence, on Saturday. The body was interred at Usk Parish Church on Sunday in the presence of a large congrega- tion, amid tokens or great respect and sympathy. The funeral was'a military one. LONGEVITY rit WALES.—The death is announced, from Llanyerwys, of a widow, named Mary Davies, at the age of 104 years. She was born at Gvrnoodfadwr, in the parish of Llanddybaefi, in 1783, and had for half a cen- tury resided on the Welsh hills at Llethyr. She was in good heetth and able to move about freely until about six months before her death, and was able to read her Welsh Bible to the last Eleven centerlarians have died in the Principality during the past three years. A shocking occurrence is reported from Sneinton, near Nottingham. A boy, named William Bingham, aged twelve years, residing at that place, was sent upstairs at his home, on Saturday, as a punishrhent for having been too long gone upon an errand. Shortly afterwards his mother entered the room where he was, and found him suspended by a cord from the bed-post.. Although he was immediately removed and medical aid summoned, all efforts failed to restore animation.

Arrrisi-rxo Munnsa ne LONDON.—What is believed to be an attempted murder took place on Saturday in W.l- - London. Early in the morning a man went to a house in Henshaw-street, Rodney-road, Walworth, and knocked the occupants up. Upon a man presenting him- self at the door, the man is said to have attacked him with a knife and stabbed him in the neck. He then escaped. The police were communicated with, and the injured man was taken to Guy's Hospital. The Fradulent Trade Marks' Committee met On Monday, Baron de Worms presiding. Mr. Courtenay Boyle, an assistant-Fecretary of the Board of Trade, who had charge of the patents and designs, was first examined. He said attention was called two years ago to the fact *that German roods were sold in England and elsewhere under Sheffield trade marks. The Act of 1662 was mainly inoperative because, instead of being summary, proce- dure Us by indictment. . *Dram OF LADY HOWITID OF GLOSBOP.—Considerable gloom hung over Glossop and neigbbourhoodon Sunday by the announcement by telegrams of the death of Lady Howard in Paris. Her ladyship had gone abroad for the benefit of her health, accompanied by Lord Howard, of Glossop, to whom she-was married about four years ago. A son and daughter are issue of the marriage. The news was unexpected, following so quickly the death of the Duchess of Norfolk. Flags areflying half-mast at Glossop Hall and on public buildings. To the Roman Catholics bar ladyship was exceedingly liberal. MtrrnartNo Carrr.E tat DERBYSTIIIIE.—The extensive :dairy farm premises of Mr. Thomas Skidmore, King Sterndale, near Buxton, were visited on Sunday night by some evil-disposed persons, who entered the shippons and deliberately out off the ends of the tails of 41 cows.

Some verT sharp instalment must have been used, the hair—a mixture of red and white—being cut close to the stump. Mr. Skidmore estimates that over 20 pounds of hair must have bean removed. No clue has been as yet discovered, but the matter is in the hands of Superinten- dent Hallam.

il-nist----iii-ortest Sure CANAL. - The following is from the circular of Messrs. Martin and Phillips:— The proposed Birmingham Ship Canal Scheme is beginning to take shape, and promises to become a reality. The estimated cost is now put at about £2,000,000, and it is suggested that this sum might be obtained by the three towns, Birmingham, Worcester, and Gloucester, combining to raise it upon the security of their rates. If the capital was got at say 34- per cent., the annual charge would be only £70,000. Towards this the receipts of the Sharpness Docks, taken at their present average, would furnish £4-0000, leaving only £30.000 to be met from the additional traffic. This sum would be realised from an additional traffic of 300,000 tons. And it seems not unreasonable to expect that the canal will secure enough traffic to pay this charge.

ALARMING F/RE IN LONDON : MARVELLOUS ESCAPE.— At 2 30 a.m. on Faturday, a fire, which resulted in the destruction of a nine-roomed house and shop, and by which the inmates narrowly escaped with their lives, was discoveredon the premises of P.O. Woods, wine and spirit merchant., Holloway-road, North London. Mr. Woods and his family-were in bed at the top of the house

at the time, and were only with great dificulty aroused by a neighbour. They then dashed downstairs, but were met by a barrier of flames, and had to retrace their steps to the roof of the house, where they awaited assistance, shilieling with fear and cold. A ladder was procured, and, with the assistance of the neighbour who had already rendered such good service, and a constable, the family was rescued from the roof at a moment when the flames burnt through and completed the destruction of the building. Adjoining premises were slightly damaged. She leaves a family of nine REPORT OF VIE CH= INSPFCTOR OF FACTORIES.—Mr. Redgrave's ieport of the work oZ the Inspectors of Fee- tones and Workshops during 11388 gives, like that of previous years, an account of the condition of businesS in the various manufacturing industries of the 'United Kingdom. In a summary estimate of the state of trade as ishovrn in the reports of the local inspectors, Mr. Red- grave states that in the latter part of the year there was "a growing feeling of confidence" in nearly all branches of industry. In Bradford the year had witnessed a. steady increase of activity, with indications of permanent rather than of spasmodic improvement. Shipbuilding on the Clyde has also shown signs of revival, and generally the despondent tone previously observable in the manufac- turing districts was less strong. The account given of the cotton industry by Mr. Coles, superintending in- spector for Lancashire and Ireiand, says :—" Since I for- warded to you my animal report last year there has been, 13= rbd to say, cosiderable improvement in many of the trade in my district. In cotton, which is the staple article of industry in the English ___,Part of -rny division, the weaving trade has greatly revrvume' and owing to this the wages of the operatives employed Is it have been advanced. In Burnley, which is the great seat of cotton weaving, there has been an average hicrease in wages of 71r per cent., and the trade there and in the district around it is exceedingly active. Le additions are being made to the weavireg mills of the'town and neighbourhood, and I am given to under- stand Unfit in one weavinz shod near Burnley a profit of 30 per cart dating the last quarter has been made. The cotton Vain trade, however, presents a very different aspect, and there appears to be a thorough stagnation in the yarn market. According to an ofgcial share list, redln a Manchester newsPoPer last July, there were Oidham Joint Stock Cotton Spinning Companies, each having an adverse balance, the total amount of which was 4234,437. In Bolton, with a view of combat- tingthe continued depressieu in the cotton trade the short time movement has been recently adopted in very many mina. The woollen trade, what I have of it in my district, seems very brisk. In the Lancashire engineering and iron trades there appears a more hopeful tone. Some of the boiler makers are fairly busy. The makers ,of cotton machinery are generally not dining mash, I especially aa regards mule spinning machinery.'

In acknoatedging a resolution of the Scottish Conven- tion of Koval Burghs, Mr. Goschen writes he is glad te observe the Convention, while pronouncing in favour of • -.onable reforms in local government, such as men of all parties can approve, has set its face against any proposal regarding Scotland which would be calcu- lated to weaken the integrity of the United Kingdom.— Mr. Gladstone, in a similar acknowledgment, simply writs—"l beg to thank you for your obliging com- munication." It is stated that Mr. I3orlase, M.P. for St. Austell Division, is likely to definitely retire from Perlis- tnent after the passing of the Coercion Bill, there being other reasons besides his health which will lead hire to take this course. The Liberal Unionist candidate will be Mr. Brydges Willyams, who sat for some years as the representative of East Cornwall, and also of Truro, and who has definitely decided to stand. The Gladnonian candidate will be Sir Arthur Hayter, at one tima.repre- sentative of Bath. Mr. Bright has addressed the following letter to a cor- respondent who proposed that that there should be este tif laws for all parts of the Empire I think your scheme is quite impracticable uncles present, if not under any, circumstances. Ireland is the victim of a con- spiracy which is in origin and object political, and the case must be dealt with having this object in view. There is no need for a change of law in Great Britain. In Ire- land a change is needed, and the Government, whether under Lord Salisbury or Mr. Gladstone, ought to be supported. No Government asks for any change in the law, except under the stringent pressure of existing disorder. To ask for it when not needed makes a Go- vernment unpopular, and tends to destroy it. The in- formation of the Government is more complete than that of any other party or person, and they ask Parlia- ment to grant increased powers. I am willing to grant them; I was once before asked to grant them, in 1881 and IslB2. lam willing to grant them now to a Govern- ment which exist and rules by right of a parliamentary majority of more than 100, returned by the household suffrage constituency 90 lately as the month of July last year. I thus give you a short explanation of my view of the present situation." Mr. Gladstone writes to Professor Stuart, chairman ef the Hyde Park Demonstration Committee, as follows "My dear Mr. Stuart,—l receive with much pleasure the resolution which proceeded from Monday's meet- ing against coercion. Its enormous mass and perfect order do the highest honour to all concerned in it, and give it an historical importance. In Ireland I am persuaded that it will have the most beneficial effect by teaching the lesson of confidence and patience, and strengthening the respect for order which has made such remarkable progress in that country. On such an occasion London does its duty as the metropolis of the country, and I trust that the mani- festations in a constitutional form of the national senti- ment may chebk the hazardous career of those who are undermining the constitution of the two islands, while they profess, and. I suppose, believe, that they are strengthening it."—Believe me, yours most faithfully, _ .

LORD SALISBURY AND THE PRIIIROSERS.—Lord SANS- bury, speaking at the fourth Grand Habitation of the Prim- rsse League at Albert Palace, London, on Wednesday, said nobody deserved more credit than the Primrose League for hearty co-operation with the Liberal Unionists at the last general election, the result of which was the defeat of tie arrogant hosts of the enemy. In assuming the attitude they did he was convinced they were sustaining the popular cease. In bringing forward the Coercion Bill tbe Govern- ment were influenced by existence of crime and intimidation in Ireland. LIBERAL CoxrEnstecz.—The National Liberal Federa- tion began a conference at Wolverhampton on Wednesday, the Right Hon. Heary Fowler, Mr. Schnadhorst. and many delegates being present. Sir Walter Foster, chairman, de- nounced the Crimes Bill, and Mr. Newbould, of Walsall, having discoursed on county organisation, it was resolved that a Liberal Council be formed for Staffordshire. Other resolutions were adopted. In the evening Mr. John Morley addressed a great meeting, dealing chiefly with the Irish question. He also !mules sharp reply to Mr. Chamberlain. SIB W. HARCOURT Ar SHORELIITCII—Str W. Harcourt, addressing a crowded meeting in Shoreditch, on Wednesday night, said the Irish question could never he got rid of by being shoved on one side nor by knocking Irishmen on the head. Referring to the so-called Parnell letter, Sir William said that when at the Home office be had as close a know- ledge as anyone except Lord Spencer of criminal associa- tions in Ireland, and he felt bound to say, in confirmation of •his Lordship's statement, that there had never come to his knowledge any evidence whatever of the participation or of the privity of the Irish members with crime in Ireland. ' MR. GLADSTONE ON THE POLITICAL

SITUATION. Mr. Gladstone was the guest of the 'Eighty Club, at Willie's Rooms, London, on Tuesday night. ktesponding to the toast of his bealth, be said he thought the time bad come when the Liberal party should take strck of their position, especially after the division of Monday night. He . . _ . and

acknowledged Lord Hartington's kindness regard to- wards old friends, but on the previous night be had charged members of the Irish party with being associated with men connected with crime. He based his statement upon cfficial Information ; but he (Mr. Gladstone) had still far greater information, and be never made such a charge. The Coer- cion Bill was a Bill against combination, not against crime. It was a Bill, in fact, against the Irish people. He denied that he had been the means of causing the negotiations to break through with regard to the Union of the Liberal party, and he could not believe that Mr Chamberlain had charged him with breaking through those negotiations, be- cause there was not one word of truth in the statement. Ho had hoped, throughout the whole of the dispute, that there- would be a reconciliation in the ranks of the Liberal party until Monday night, when he saw three score of Liberals

vote for the -CeerCion Bill, in support of which not the least evidence had been given, tier the least intimation made that the measure would be passed for ulterior purposes, namely, to make the State pay the high price which the Irish people might be called upon to pay for their holdings. He advised the Liberal party to refer the whole question to the judg- ment of the nation.

SIR G. TREVELYAN AND THE UNIONISTS. Dr. Webster, chairman of the Aberdeen Liberal Union- ist Association, has reoeived the following letter from Sir G. 0. Trevelyan, in reply to the communication of the committee's minute Of the lala inst., withdrawing the invitation to Sir George to visit Aberdeen, in conse- quence of the views' he expressed an tile Irish question: Welconabe, Stratford-on-Avon, April 16, 1887. Dear Dr. Webster,—l am obliged for your letter and for the accompanying minute of the Unionist Liberal Associa- tion. I recognise the courteous straightforward manner in which you and they have treated me. I must respect- fully refer to one passage in the secretary's letter:— Sir George explains that one main feature in his address will be nothing more or less than an adverse criticism or condemnation of the Government's Criminal Law (Ireland) Amendment Bill; a measure the defeat of which, whatevel opinion be formed on its merits, in- volves either the existence of that Government or a dis- solution.' Undoubtedly I think that public men are bound to form an opinion 011 the merits of any and every bill before they support it. Those Liberals Who opposed the Irish bills of last year justly take credit to them- selves, because, having objections to important pro- visions in those measures'; they would not support them, even in order to maintain a Liberal Government in office. I cannot agree to the position that, in order to keep a. Conservative Government in office, Liberals, or Conservatives either, are bound to refrain from judging on its merits a bill of the vital importance of that which is now on tor a second reading in the House of Corn- mons.—l remain, yours very truly (Signed), G. 0. Tawym-aw." Dr. Webster explains that the passage quoted by Sir George forms part of the minute of the associatixm. LORD HARTINGTON AND MR. CHAMBERLAIN. Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen spoke at meetings in Edinburgh on Satur lay, and Mr. Chamberlain at a meeting at Inverness. Lord Hartiegton, in acknowl,dging the pre- sentation of an address, said that in reply to the reproach that the Unionists had not proposed a policy of their own his lordship said it would have been an error of jedgmen and of policy for them to do so; but he claimed that by the praetiahalliance into which they had entered with the that Conservative party they had induced that party to propose imea.qures of remedial legislation for Ireland far in advance of anything which that party would have contemplated a therevolutionaryo ! ofew thyee Irish hago. question den could hat e arrived party in Ireland would have to be overthrown. Mr. Goschen responding to the toast of his health at a banquet, said the Government were deeply sensible of the support which they had received from the Liberal Unionists in the House. Mr. Chamberlain' replying to an address, denied tha "Ireland blocked the way." It was not, he said, Ireland f that prevented the British Parliament from doieg its work I but a section of the Liberal party. He regretted that the obstruction in the House of Commnns was due to the en- couragement which the obatrnetives received from the ! leaders of the Liberal party. He did not despair of a re conciliation of the Liberal party, but he had little hope of from its present leaders. He appealed to tb• more moderate men of the Gladstone party, if they did not agree with Mr Gladstone's proposals, to formulate their own plans and tel the Unionists what they wanted, and if they were reason- able the Unionists would adopt them. On Tuesday morning Mr. Chamberlain left Dingwall and travelled by the High- land Railway as far as Strome Ferry. The right hon. gen , tleman was accernpanied by Mr. Jesse Collings and a repre- sentative of the crofters of the district, who pointed on various glens from which tenants ha.d been evicted. The right bon. gentleman then visited a number of crofters in ' the district of Strome Ferry. On Wednesday afternoon Mr Chamberlain and Mr. Jesse Collings returned from Shiel to - Strome Ferry, and later in the day proceeded to Stoma- way.

Coercion has were.4.ltY•sixtirnes even when the Irish left to struggle against it single-

handed. Who can doubt that it will fail for the eighty-seventh time when the Irish leaders are supported by a majority of the representatives of Scotland and of Wales, and by four-fifths of the Liberal party in England? The Coercion Bill is a bad bill, a villanously bad bill, and it ought to fail. It is cowardly and tyrannical in conception, for it aims not at reducing crime—it is notorious that it will increase it—but in gagging ard manacling the constitutional representatives of the people' of Ireland. Lord HARTINGTON, who is thel prime mover in this matter, for the Tories are but his puppets, says : • i "I have taken many opportunities upon preliious occasions of saying that there is in Ireland a tevo- lutionary party which relies upon the support of the still more revolutionary party in America, who, have acquired over the minds of the people of Ire- land an undue and excessive influence which has to be contended with and which has to be over- thrown before a final development and solution can be arrived at." The revolutionary party are to b 2 overthrown, 'but who are the revolutionary party? They are the men whom the electors of Ireland, for the first time exercising the full fran- chise, have sent to this country to represent them, and to say as with one voice that they de- sire Home Rule—that they wish, to be al- lowed to manage their own affairs in their own way. They are the men, the only men, who, as General BULLER admits, have ever done anything. for the peasantry; they have stood between the tenants and starvation; they have forced grasping landlords to take their hands off the throats of famishing people, and for this offence -this daring in- terposition—they are to be driven out of the country or forced into prison, so that rapa- cious landowners may plunder the people with impunity. Lord BEACONSFIELD was right when he said a revolution in Ireland was necessary; but he wished it to be a peace- ful revolution. The Tories and the Coer- cionist Liberals do not desire that it shall be a revolution of peace; the barometer of crime is low, and they would force it higher. They cannot answer the just demands of the Nationalists; but they believe they can close their mouths by clapping them in gaol. Let them, however, beware; the day of reckoning may, after all, be nearer than they think. Pride gpeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." The English ' people are tired of the "ever poisonous and ever failing remedy; " they remember that the present House of Commons was returned ' on the strength of the cry of" No coercion ;" and when the next appeal to the ballot-box is made they will belie their best traditions if ; they do not punish those who have been guilty of a flagrant betrayal of trust.

NOBODY seems to have come very well out of the scene which took place in the House of Commons during the early hours of Satur- day morning, when Mr. HEALY was sus- pended for a week for giving Colonel SAUNDERSON the lie direct. The SPEAKER was undoubtedly right in ruling that it was an infringement of the rules of the House for one member to call another a " liar •," but after Mr. HEALY had been named and sus- pended for the offence, Mr. SEXTON made use of the same epithet; and the SPEAKER, instead of taking instant action in this case, proceeded to call on Colonel SAUNDERSON to withdraw the charge which had given rise to the bad language. In the end this was done. The fire-eating Orange member for North Armagh certainly tried to wriggle out of the corner in which he found himself pinned, but the SPEAKER left him no means ef escape. He was not in a position to justifo his charge that certain of the Nationalist members had associated with men whom they knew to be mur&rers, and he was finally compelled to withdraw his odious accusation. It was a matter of course, after that, for Mr. SEXTON to say that he withdrew the language he had used in denouncing Colonel SAUNDER- SON, and so the matter ended without the member for West Belfast being called to account. It thus happened that Mr. SEXTON was allowed to go "Scot free;" although he had not only given the lie to Col. SAUNDER- SON, but threatened him with personal chas- tisement. Mr. }ITALY on the other hand was named and suspended for a smaller offence, and this being—to say the least of it unsatisfactory—it was not unreasonable to suggest that the resolution of suspension should be rescinded. An effort to this end was made in the House on Monday night bot Mr. SMITH, on behalf of the Government, said he should oppose the proposal unless it was understood that Mr. HEALY made an apology for his 'transgression. Mr. SEXTON, on Mr. HEALY'S behalf, offered to withdraw the offensive language used, if Colonel SkUN- DERSON would withdraw the foul charge he had made. The member for North Armagh seemed, however, in a milky mood ; he fenced with the issue; and delivered himself of a bungling statement which made confu- sion worse confounded. Mr. GLADSTONE intervened twice to give him an opportunity of setting himself right ; but Colonel SAUNDERSON had had enough of eating his own words; and was too little of a gentle- man to withdraw, when not compelled •to withdraw, a charge which he could not sub- stantiate. In the course of the discussion. Mr. JACOB BamErr pertinently asked how it happened that, as two members of the House had committed what might be called the same offence, one was suspended while the other was allowed to keep his seat. This brought the SPEAKER to his feet with an explanation to the effect that Mr. HEALY made use of offensive language when he was not directly implicated in the charge made by Colonel SKUNDERSON in other words, the SPEAKER had taken into account the greater provoca- tion which Mr. SEXTON subsequently received. This may be creditable to the SPEAKER'S good feeling; but it ought surely to have had nothing to do with the technical grounds of his ruling. The unparliamentary language was as much an offence against the rules of the House in one case as the other; and we cannot but think it would have been better if the SPEAKERIhad taken Colonel SAUNDER- SON to task in the first instance. We do not, of course, defend the language used by Mr. HEALY and Mr. SEXTON; but their offence was trivial compared with that of the mem- ber who made an abominable chatge without being able to support it with a particle of evidence. But tis ever the way with these Orangemen ; their gallant colonels are any- thing but gallant; they talk of lining the ditches, but when they are boldly con- fronted it is found that they much prefer to skulk behind hedges.

MR. SETON-KA.RR, the member for Sr. Helens, intervened in the debate on the Coercion Bill on Friday night, and contrived to talk a considerable amount of. nonsense in a comparatively short space of time. In the course of his speech, he said : There were hundreds and thousands of Irish working-men who did not care two straws about Home Rule, who had no sympathy with the National League, or with that expression which

hon. members below the gangway were so fond ofl using—lrish nationality. But there was one thing i they did care about—to obtain honest employment. These unemployed Irishmea now found themselVes, ' by the operations& the National League, destitute, and the first place they came to was the county of Lancaster, where were tthe Lancashire operatives and artisans, and ran down the rate of wages. He did not complain for a moment of the Irish work- ing-men doing this, but he did complain or the operation of the National League, which, by coerc- ing the people, endangering individual liberty, and by driving capital out of the country, drove these people to England, who might otherwise have been happy and prosperous and obtained employment in their own country. He referred to Sir Redvers Bul- ler's evidence, which stated that in a district of Killarney there were 1,685 acres of farm land on which grass was growing, from 950 acres of which tenants had been evicted..

Mr. SETO/I-KARR Ms/ be blind, or he would perceive chat he is answered out of his own mouth. Who evicted the tenants from the oso acres? And why were they evicted? These poor people were turned out of their houses to die in ditches, or to make their way to Lancashire if they could, not by members of the National League, but by the landlords who were exacting impossible rents. When the member for St. Helens quotes Sir RED- VERS BULLER, why does he not let it be known that this humane' representative of an inhuman Government frankly acknowledges that nothing was done for the tenants until the Nationalists came to their aid ? Give Ireland Home Rule; let the tenants have security for their holdings by a just land bill which does not require that they shall become bankrupt in order to assert their rights, and it will soon be found that Irishmen, whose love of Ireland is a passion, will go back to the land of their birth to increase and multiply, and make fruitful the earth. But this cannot be whilst there are so many landlords' tools— so many Seton-Karrs and Gilbert Greenalls in the House. The men of Lancashire must bestir themselves; they must, as soon as they can, set aside the Coercionists and put men of Conciliation in their place.

The exhibition of the model of the Ship Canal has been a great treat. It has brought the scheme home in a way which nothing else could do; and we are rint surprised to hear that, wherever the model is shown, there is an increase in the demand for shares. The people of Warrington prick up" when they see how well they figure in the matter of dock accommodation. It suggests a time when the town will be greater and the rates less. Meantime a large portion of the third million remains to be raised in a very short time ; so pray put your names down for big , figures—you who have a good balance at the bankers.

At Widnes, they don't seem to be very jubilant as to the Jubilee. There was not a little hesitation at a meeting of the School Board, on Tuesday. about taking part with other School Boards in a joint address to her Majesty, congratulating her on the progress which had been made in education during the fifty years of her reign, After a good deal of talk, small and large, the discussion was adjourned. Really, the members of the Widnes Board might give a trifle. If they will not subscribe anything else, they might at least subscribt their signatures.

From the evidence given at the inquest on the body of the boy who was drowned in a brickfield in Warrington, on Saturday, it would seem that consciousness might have been restored if there had not been lamentv ble negligence consevent upon lamentable ignorance. As the Coroner remarked, it is an absurd idea to suppose that a body must not be touched until someone in authority has seen it. It would be a good thing if the children at our elementary schools were taught something about restoratioa from drowning. It might prove as useful to them as a; knowledge of the mountains of the moon.

Mouses Missions To SEAMEN., BUNO)RN.—The annual concert in aid of the Runcorn Branch of the !limey Mis- sions to Seamen, was given in Runcorn Public Hall ow Monday night, by the band of the Indefatigable Training I Ship. The instramentak performances of the band as a;I whole, and the vocal selections of irelividual members, were well rendered and much enjoyed. The chairman (the Rev. W. Many- efforts had been made of late years to effect their mental, moral, and physical improve- ment, and the Mersey Missions to Seamen had taken a prominent part. The Runcorn Mission, co they knew, was presided over by Mr. W. Shaw, whose report for the past year showed that he had paid 9,000 visits to boatmen and their families, and during thesel visits had addressed 11,000 persons. (Applause.) In addi- , lion 197 meetings had been held, and 12,000 persons ad- dressed. Then there were open air meetings and Band of Hope and temperance meetings; and besides there was that important work of the Sunday school. He was sure that those present could not support a better cause than the Mersey Missions. (Applause.) The concert concluded with the customary votes of thanks. THE MANCHESTER EXHIBITION. --:SatisfactorY progress was made on Wednesday with the work of arranging and fixing the various exhibits. The I work of installation will now be carried on with increased vigour. • The authorities are anxious to have everything in place as soon as possible in order that the building may be suitably decorated in readiness for the opening day. The decorators are making satisfactory progress with the interior of the dome, and • also with the rockery and, the fountain in the centre of the floor, and there ean be no doubt that the general effect will he at once very striking and exceedingly pleasing During the time the exhibition remains open articles manufactured within the building will be allowed to be sold and removed, but no exhibit will be suffered to be taken away without the written permission of the general manager. The seats for the opening ceremony on the 3rd prox. are now be- ing allotted as speedily as possible.

MODEL OF SHIP CANAL AT WARRINGTON.—The large model of the ship canal was on view at the Pub- lic Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday, and was there seen by thousands of persons. The model is carved in wood, and gives in miniature a very clear idea of the length and course of the canal, and of the physical features of the country through which the proposed waterway is to run. The relative posi- tions of the canal and the various towns past which it will run, e.nd the provisions that will be made to meet the requirements of these different places were also geographically indicated. In the course of the afternoon several explanatory ad- dresses were given by Mr. Hunter, in whose charge the model was, and various diagrams were also hung round the room, and contained a good deal of infoimation as to the engineering features of the canal. In the evening the hall was continuously crowded by,people eager to see the model. It should be mentioned that in the afternoon Mr. Leader Williams, the chief engineer of the Scheme, was present, and gave short address on the,pro- ject. 34 , THE MEMBER FOR NEWTON DIVISION ON IRE- LAND.—At a public meeting in connection with the Primrose League, held at Golborne, Mr. T. W. Legh, , M.P., said the Irish question hung an the political , horizon like a huge cloud, and as the result of the Plan of Campaign society in ' Ireland had become utterly disorganised and demoralised. The result was agrarian crime, failure of justice, and boycotting, any one of which was sufficient justification to warrant a change in the law. But when those three evils were combined, the change was absolutely required. From the arguments of the Separatists people would be inclined to think the Crimes Bill was one of the most unjust measures that was ever passed, . and that the Government were about to trample on the Irish people. He maintained that there was hardly a nation on the face of the earth that enjoyed greater liberties than did Ireland. They were not burdened by a State church, they could vote by ballot, and they had a free Press. As to the tenants, they enjoyed privi- leges which no English tenant enjoyed. He was sure that the present bill was an honest attempt to settle the difficulty in Ireland, and that was the reason why he voted for it. He believed the rata would justify the action of those who were iesponsible fot it. Speaking on Wednesday evening, at Billinge. near Wigan, Mr. Legh said he was of opinion that much of the Irish difficulty had been caused by spasmodic attempts at what was called remediul legislation. He thought the present attempt of the Government was a genuine and honest effort to settle the ques- tion for the time being, and he believed that the Government and those who supported them had acted in full justice, and that they were and would be fully justified. •

CHA.NCELLOR ESPIN AT W.kIIItINGTpN.—Oti Wed- nesday morning • the Worshipful aancellor Espiri delivered bis, charge to the 6,p.rchwardens and sidesmen of the district, elected. at the recent vestry meetings at the Warrington Parish Church. Having spoken at some length with reference to the dispo- sal of church receipts, and touched upon the , sub- jects of church reform, and of the Church Patron- age Bill now before the House of Lords, Chancellor Bspin olmer wed that he had been asked to state what qualified a person to have a vote and voice t a vestry meeting, and what sort of person could be legally elected a Churchwarden. To questions like these he could not give a general answer. In most parishes the minister named one warden, and the householders elected the other. The churchwarden, •according to the Act 8 and 9 Vic., chap. 70, should be " fit person," bat it did not appear to be strict- ly necessary that the churchwardens themselves should be householders cr ratepayers .in the dis- trict,thettgh there never had, so far as he kirew, been any definition of lag- on what the term "fit person meant. Ile would remark that if any ob- leation -was to be made tci, 'any person appointed churchwarden, such objection shotild, if possible; he entered in the minutes of the vestry meeting, as it 'Might be too tate to bring forward an objection on :the *ay of visitation, when the churchwardens I were to be admitted. Pre thought that some reform was wanted in districts like the one in which they were met. It was an anomaly that in a new parish the -householders had a right to 'elect their 'own churchwardens, and, still retained the right to go to the veary of the parish church, although they might have long ceased to worship at that church, or to tonaribUte to its funds. Oa the other ltd the parishioners he the old parish had no viglit in the new one. His advice on this and other matters ef Church reform was that they should keep a watclifill eye, and attend the zuri-decatuil and the Idiocesan conferences, where these subjects •we explained and discussed. STIMPLECILONNG AT lIMIRDOCIK PAUL—The new ventane of the Ilaydock Park 'Authorities, on Sat- urday afternoon, was for a wonder smiled upon by the weather arta a beautifully fine and 'spring-Bhp day 'favoured their steeplechase gathering. The programme issued was, however, not a wery tempt- ing one, the 'multiplicity of hunt meetings during ' the pest fortnight having no doubt thoroughly ex- hausted theequine material, and the attendance, thong% proving by its largeness how much more popular than coursing racing is, was yet a long way below the merits of the beautifully-situated grounds and ..'the pleasant sport provided, There were plenty of visitors from Liverpool, St. Helens, Wigan, Warrington, Manchester, and the surrounding towns., and the commodious stands and enclosures were-well patronised by the gentry of the neigh- bourhood, amongst whom were Sir Humphrey de Trafford, and 'Messrs. E. J.Thornewill, R. 'F. 'Glad- stone,sil. F. Fawcett, L Hartley Bibby, 'J. Henry Stock,`T..Stone, A. Hassell, T. B. Walford, A. F. Pope,'E. Stone, 'Major Currie, .and Captain Baldwin. Mr. A. Brocklehirst acted as steward hi place of Mr. Lee], M.P., whilst Mr. Thernewill supplied the place of Mr. C. J. F. Fawcett. A capital race track lof a mile and a half in circumference had been laid out under the supervision of Mr. R. I. Anson,,everY 'jump on which could easily be seen by the specta- ltars, whlst the speed of thehorses could be amply tested by a fine straight run in of nearly half a mile, and no doubt when the fine course is thoroughly known to the owners of horses there will be no lack of entries on any future occasion. The pro- gramme, on Saturday, was not a very strong one, only six events with thirty-eight entries figuring thereon. This was further reolueed by the tailing through of the Llayilock Steeplechase, for which only one competitor was on the ground. The ex- ecutiae offered .C 25 for a walk over, which was foolishly declined by the owner lest his horse, Lot- tery, should in consequence have to carry a penalty for the last race, which, by the way, he did not showing ones more the truth of the old saw, "that a bird in the hand's worth two in the bush." IThe results of the 'various events were that the New- ton maiden hunters' steeplechase plate of 40 sovs.was WO n by Mr. B. Jay's Recovery; the Garswood hunters' selling plate of 40 sovs. iy Mr. C. 11. Wil- son's Corvette; the Golborne selling hunters' steeple- chase plate of 40 sovs. by Mr., Brocklehurst's Iron- master; the hunters' plate of 50 sot's. by Mr. W. Goode's Geranium ; and the united hunters' steeplechase plate of 60 sevs, by Mr, Wallace's relaar.

THE CORONERSHIP FOR THE HONOR AND FREgoF HALTON.—Mr. T. J. Ridgway, solicitor, of Wareirig- ton, who for 15 years held the appointment of coro- ner for the honor and fee of Helton, some time ago placed his resignation before the Duchy of Lahcas- ter. The Chancellor of he 'Duchy has appointed Mr. J. E. Worsley to the vacant post. Mr. Worsley has for 12 years acted as deputy-coroner, and his ap- pointment has given the highest satisfaction in the district On Wednesday afternoon Mr. ' Worsley held his firstinquiry as coroner, at the Half-way • House, Halton-road, Runcorn. At the close, Mr. WorsleY informed the jury that Mr. Ridgway had resigned the•_office of coroner. The Chancel- lor of the Duchy of Lancaster ad been plead to appoint Mm' (At. Whrsley) in his .phice. During the twelve,years, he (Mr. Worsley) Mid acted as deputy7borofier he hadneier,experienced anything but tie _greatest kindness and assistance from every jury, associated with . him, as well as from the medical men who had been called in, the solicitors who had been engaged when occasion required, and the superintendents and officerso.tif police. He only hoped, now he was the coroner, they would extehd to 'him the same consideration. and courtesy which had been extended to him ddr- ing the time he was deputy-coroner. (Hear, hear. f Mr. *. T. J. Waterworth '(foreman of the jury), said that on behalf of the jury he had very great plea- sure in congratulating Mr. Worsley upon his new 'appointment—Dr. McDougall said that, as one wilco had attendedinquests for the last 18 years, they would perhaps allow him .to add his testimony to the conscientious manner in which Mr. Ridgway had discharged his duties as coroner for the homer and fee of Halton. A more conscientious, or a mdre just man it would be impossible to find. He hear- tily congratulated Mr. Worsley upon the appoint-. ment. (Applause.)—The Coroner said he was - tremely obliged for the kind expressions which h d been given utterance to, respecting his friend li4;r. Ridgway. He, shoujd endeavdur %%make as goocl,a coroner as Mr. Ridgway, bad made, and if he did that he should satisfy himself, and he should also satisfy them. (Applause.)

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Shakespere, who knew everything, antici- pated the Primrose League, for he speaks of "the primrose path of dallianVe " and " the primrose way to the everlasting bon- fire,"

Why is it that the Tories are full of "nods ,and becks, and wreathed smiles" on Prim- rose Day? Do they really rejoice on the anniversary of the death of Lord Beaconsfield? And is it because he once said that a Con- servative Government was an "organised hypocrisy ?" It was stated last night in the House of Commons that "to secure the neutrality of the Government. the Church of England had been disestablished in Ceylon." We have never before been so much in love with "neutrality." Couldn't we have a taste of it in this country, and with a similar object ?

Mr. Goschen's Budget is hard on the memory of the late Lord Iddesleigh, who, as Sir Stafford Northcote, established the Sinking Fund which the present Chancellor of the Exchequer sets aside to make sure of a surplus. It was Sir Stafford who added fourpeme to the tobacco duty, and it is Mr. Goschen who knocks it off. Sus- pending payment of debt is, it may be noted. a peculiar, but not az unusual way with impecunious people of ensuring cash in hand.

Colonel Saunderson, referring to the recent scene in the House, says he felt that the time had come when "somebody must bell the Fenian cat." He certainly began the opera- tion ; but as the world now knows this brave militiaman finked, and backed out. Had he not better mind what he is about ? Besides belling the Fenian cat, there may be such a thing as muzzling the Orange dog. The signs of rabies are certainly not • absent.

Lord Hartington lost his head—and it -is a \ -very unusual thing for him to do—when, re- ferring to the " Times " atttacks on the Par- nellites, he said:. "All they have to do is to give a conclusive demonstration of the Tin- truth of these charges " ; that is to say the Parnellites have to set about proving a nega- tive. "A" calls B" dishonest, and "C's " notion of fairness is that "B" should proceed to prove the " untruth " of the charge. Really this is absurd. "The burden of proof," as Mr. Gladstone says, " lies on those who make the charge."

Lova Hartington is "hard set" against the Nationalists; and so far as the Government are concerned he N the driving shaft in the matter of coercion. Rightly or wrongly, the idea has taken bossession of him that the Parnellites have been associated with crime in Ireland. He speaks of his official know- ledge; but Lord Spencer and Mr. Gladstone have quite as much official knowledge as the member for Rossendale, and they acquit the Parnellites of the charge. Lord Hartington, it is perhaps as well to remember, lost a brother in Ireland by the knife of assassins; and it may be that the memory of that terrible tragedy warps his judgment.

But no such plea can be set up on behalf of Mr. Chamberlain, who is trying to see how much Liberal Unionists will stand in the way of indirect abuse of Mr. Gladstone. He is somebody certainly, but when he tries to put himself on a level with the Grand Old Man, he somehow looks ridiculously small. Speaking of him at the banquet of the Eighty Club, on Tuesday, Mr. Gladstone said :

I am told Mr. Chamberlain has stated it is a matter beyond question that certain communications aim- ing at a 'reconciliation among Liberals were broken off 'because I had announced I would submit to no deviation ist the billor in the provisions of the bills which were introduced last year. It is my duty to disbelieve that Mr. Chamberlain has ever made such a statement, for, gentlemen, I gay, in the face of the world, there is not a word of truth in it.
That statement lays the member for West Birmingham on his back, and there we may , let him lie.

Colonel King-Harman, the new Under- Secretary for Ireland, winces under the re- minder that he was a Home Ruler in 870. He says Home Rule was an absolutely dif- ferent thing to what it is now. Well, it cer- tainly never was better, or had better pros pects, and the infererce is that it is Colonel King-Harman wno has degenerated. The Home Secretary is also an ex-Home Ruler. It is "a pretty sight" to watch these members of the Ministry denounce their old love. Renegades? Oh dear, no; there is no such word now-a-days.

There is a good deal in the art of putting a thing. Sir W. C. Brooks, speaking at Lymm, on Tuesday, said that in voting for the Coercion Bill he gave a vote in support of the Government of the day in their effort to restore our long-suffering Irish fellow

WARRINGTON "A " v. BOOTLE lsr.—This match Was played at Warrington, on Saturday. The home team were poorly represented, havicg to play eight second team men. Whittle kicked off for Warrington, and after a while Molyneux, Jones, and Eyes improved matters for Warring- ton by dribbling to the visitors' line, but Roberts relieved by a good kick into touch. Warburton and Unsworth again caused the visitors some anxiety, but Balmer cleared by punting to Appleton, who made a short return. Molyneux and Jones next broke away from the scrimmage and drib- bled to the line, having hard lines in not scoring, the ball going dead. Hicks dropped eat, play resting in centre. Foster, Teare, and Wilson came away with a rush, but Ap- pleton secured cad put in a nice ran and kick, and follow- ing ap prevented a return. The Bootle forwards took play to centre, Brown saving. Fox now passed to Bailey, who put in a good kick, Brown returning into touch. Whittle next passed to Boardman, who made a good run and kick Into touch. Some good passing between the Bootle backs was now witnessed, Bailey kicking to Browa, who made a short return. The Bootle forwards worked the ball to the home line, where some tight scrimmaging took place, War- rington being forced to touch down. Warburton dropped out, Balmer returning to Brown, who kicked to Roberts, but through off-side tackling on the part of Appleton, the ball was scrimmaged near the line, the home players having again to touch down. Boardman dropped out, and the visitors worked the oval to the Warrington 25, where Larkin got possession, and passed nicely to Balmer, who dropped a splendid goal. When half time was called the score stood— Bootle I dropped goal and 2 minors to Warrington 3 minors. Balmer restarted, and Brown failing to return, he had to save by touching down. Warburton dropped out. Balmer returning to Bate, who was allowed a free kick, nothing tangible resulting. Shortly afterwards Fox passed to Bal- mer, who kicked over the line Brown having again to touch down. A lot of passing now took place between the Bootle men, but the tackling of the home team prevented them , getting far, and Boardman getting hold, put in a splendid rtn- and kick, Riddock having to concede another minor point. Balmer dropped out, and the ball being charged down, Unsworth WAS instrumental in taking play to the visitors' 25, where Whittle gained possession and passed to Boardman, this player again dropping at goal. Riddock touching down. Balmer dropped out, and from a loose scrimmage Bate passed to Whittle, this player repassing to Boardman, who put in a good kick, but Bailey returned well. Whittle next made a dodgy run, and passed to Board- man, the latter player almost getting over. By good pass- ing the visitors cleared their lines, and Bailey pat in a strong run and passed to Roberts, this player being collared by Unsworth. Whittle again secured the ball, and passed nicely to Boardmao—this player, after a brilliant run, gain- ing a grand try, Warburton making a good attempt at goal. Balmer kicked off, but through the visitors' forwards getting off-side, the ball was scrimmaged in Bootle quarters, and Bailey getting hold, put in a short run, and kicked to touch. Fox now came nicely round the scrimmage, and kicked to Brown, who missed the ball, but Whittle rushed up and put in a splendid punt, play resting in the Bootle quarters. Spedding and Barber dribbled to centre, but the borne front rank, headed by Jones, Eyes. and Molyneaux, again took play to the visitora' quarter-flag, where Whittle secured and ran round the scrimmage and passed to the forwards, who dribbled to the line, Warburton succeeding in getting over The same player failed at the place kick. RUNCORN v. BRADFORD —The Runcorn Committee hav- ing received an invitation from the Bradford Club to play at Park Avenue ground, the team journeyed thither on Saturday hat, arriving ahout two o'clock. They were met at the station by Mr. Richardson, acting secretary of the Bradford Club, who had vehicles ready to convey the teanc to the ground. Runcorn were unfortunately without Speakman, Wright and Cawley ; Bradford being minus Ritchie, Wilkineon, and Wright. About 8,000 spectators bad assembled to vritnese the match. W. Hughes kicked off at 3-20, and Bonsor returned. Sutcliffe made a good taunt, Woods, however, relieving to centre. Good exchasgee by Hawcridge and Bonsor got the ball to Runcorn 25, and P. Robertson ran in, but Haigh failed at the place kick. A fine ran by H. Hughes was deservedly cheered ; he then passed to Wainwright, and the latter to Galley, Who brought play well into Bradford weeders. Hickson put in a dribble, but Woods frustrated his endeavours to score. Lunt and Robertshaw exchanged kicks, and Potter directly afterwards scored the second try for Bradford, Haigh not improving the score. Runcorn now pulled themselves together, Broady following the drop out, splendidly tackling Sutcliffe with the ball in his hands. Waiewright, Ford, and Lewis dribbled to their opponents' goal line, and from a throw in W. Hughes forced himself over the line, Woods kicking a goal. After the kick at ceetre, Critchley picked up nicely and Lunt just as nicely tackled him. Barns and Andrews by short runs gained ground for Runcorn, and Clarke dribbled further on. Sutcliffe was awarded a free kick, which lodged play in mid-field. Davis next had a clever run rounding the forwards and finishing by good punt to the home 25; Faulkner also had a free kick, considerable ground, being gained thereby. Bonsor, however, retaliated, only being stopped by Woods. Later a dead ball WAS regis- tered for Vradford. Hicksoa restarted the game, Hutchin- son dribbling well to the Runcorn goal line, liolme causing a touchdown to be conceded to Bradford. The ball was directly taken to Bradford 25 by Riley, W Hughes, Andrews, Gatley, and Wahowright, and the latter gained a most unmistakeable try, and although the whistle had not been blown the referee ruled the ball back. A. huge punt by Sutcliffe sent the ball to Lunt, who judiciously put it Into touch. Hawcridge now became very dangerous, his dodging being grand, hut Lust collared him finely. H Hughes got possession after a hard scrimmage and gave the ball to Davies, and Wainwright receiving it from the latter, got past the backs and obtained a try. Woods again kicked a neat goal. Bonser, Hawcridge„ and Critcbley passed well to each other, and equally as good play by Clarke, Broady, W Hughes, and Riley was ap- plauded by a very impartial lot of spectators. Several rushes by the Bradford forwards took play into mid-field, Faulkner, Barns, and Davies averting danger. Critchley, though, managed to scramble behind the Runcorn goal line, but on an appeal the referee decided that he had been pushed into touch in goal before grounding the ball. After several tough scrimmages, however, Hawcridge gained a try, Sutcliffe kicking a good goal. A finely-contested game ended in a victory for Runcorn by two goals to Bradford one goal, twe tries, and four minor pdints. For the winners, Woods at full back was safer than Sutcliffe on the other side, and Riley, Davies, and Lunt did their work well. Too much praise cannot be given the latter for his fine tackling. Hughes and Andrews worked liked Trojans, and of the forwards W Hughes, Broady, and Wainwright were ever to the front. On the other aide Hawcridge, Bonsor, and Hickson were towers of strength, their play being of the highest order. After the match the teams were enter- tained at the Talbot Hotel, and Mr. Richardson, in propos- ing the health of the Runcorn Football Club, said he hoped they might arrange fixtures with each other for next season, and also expressed himeelf highly delighted with the exhi- bition of the game, remarking the great similarity in the style of play of Runcorn and Bradford. Teams—Runcorn : Woods, fullback; Davies, Riley, and Lunt, three-quarter backs; Andrews and II Hughes (captain), half backs; W Hughes, W g Broady, W Faulkner, J Lewis, J Clarke, J Barns. J Gatlev, G Wainwright, and J Ford. forwards. Bradford: Sutcliffe, full back; Hawcridge, P Robertshaw, and Holmes, three-quarter backs; Bonsor (captain) and Critchley, half backs; Hickson, Haigh, Nelson, Potter, J Robertshaw. Moore, M. Bonsor, Gray, and Hutchinson, forwards. Umpires :—Runcorn : Mr. W. Wright ; Brad- ford : Mr. Perkins. Referee : Captain Risbworth, of Keighley. WEST LANCASHIRE V. WESTMORELAND.

' The return match between the above unions was played ' at Widnes, on Thursday evening, the weather being damp, and the attendance numbering 2000., The visitors came without several of the best forwards, and it was 6-25 before Smith, of Widnes, the West Lancashire captain, who offi- ciated in place of Hughes, of Runcorn, kicked off against a slight wind. Hulme punted On, and West Lancashire looked like scoring, when the visitore came right away, anti the result of some excellent passing on the part of West- moreland's three-quarter backs was that Walker almost got a try, but a touchdown was the only result. From the drop- out Broady. Smith, and Turner were prominent in a dribble ' for the home team, but Walker getting bold, kicked to the home full back, who in a remarkable manner fumbled the ball, and Beetham, racing up quickly, ran the ball behind the West Lancashire line, and Cross as Promptly placed the goal. Nettled by this reverse, the Lancastrians played up, but a grand dribble by Nicholson and Wilkinson almost the length of the ground caused the home players to resort to a touchdown. After the drop out Jolley distin- guished himself with a fine run, kick, and follow up, whilst a supplementary effort from Elulme caused Westmoreland to touchdown, and directly afterwards a fast dribble, headed by Parr, Smith, and Broady, caused a second minor to be registered for Lancashire; whilst a minute later a touch in coal went against the visitors. Here rilkington, of St. Helens, put in a fine run, and after Smith bad nearly scored, Armstrong put in a fine run down the centre, and passed to Nicholson, who got over, but losing the ball, left it for Wilkinson to complete the try. Walker made a poor attempt at goal, and was also at fault after Berry had secured another try for the visitors Directly after change of ends Westmoreland were whistled back when on the line, and then Pilkington (St. Helens), Barnes, and Broady transferred operations to the other end, where Armstrong, cleverly getting a pass intended for Jolley raced three-parts the length of the field, and gained a fine try, which Cross did not improve upon. The ball had been hardly put in motion again before Davies put in a fine run, and Smith, Whittle, and Monks were to the fore with a fine dribble, which caused the visitors to save. Then Holmes dashed in and got a try for West Lancashire and Broady placed a goal. In the remaining stages of the game Walker put in a fine bit of play, and Barnes effected two remarkably fine runs, in one case passing to Davies, who kicked, followed up, and tackled the Westmoreland full back over his own line. CRICKET,

Taken all round, the Warrington lads played a grand combined game, the steady determined play of the forwards proving one too many for the strong combination of the Rangers' backs. When they set out the visitors thought they would come back beaten, but they were well pleased with themselves when they made it a drawn game. Nevins, for the first time, played full back with the first team, and infused a lot of energy into-his play, kicking coelly and tackling with great determination. Undoubtedly Barnes was the pick of the trio of three quarters, although Massey played extremely well. The two half backs played a fine game, Warren running round the scrimmage several times and putting in some fine rushes. Speakman, on the other hand, saved well, and had a good man to contend against when playing against Simpson. Perhaps Davies and Little- wood were the pick of the forwards. The Rangers were best represented by Robertson, Veale, and Simpson behind, and McGowan, Teggin, and Atkinson forward. The local junior competition started by the Warrington Football Club has se, far proved a success in every respect. The number of entrances is large, and the matches that have taken place on every night this week have been well attended by spectators. It is quite evident, even apart from the premier club, that there is a large reserve of foot- ball talent In Warrington.

An indication that tha football season is rapidly drawing to a close, is to be found in the comparative infrequency of matches of an important nature. About all the cup compe- titions have been fought out, and these having been decided, the enthusiasum of the players is naturally beginning to decline. In addition to the matches of the local teams, two of the most important was the meeting of Broughton and Salford, and Swinton and Moseley. In the former match neither of the teams were fully represented, but a good con- test was witnessed, Salford coming out with seven minors against two for their opponents, Swinton upheld their old reputation in their encounter with Moseley, winning by one goal, one try, and two minors to two minors. Under Association rules and in splendid weather the picked representatives of Lancashire met the champions of united Ulster on Saturday, at Belfast. The Laacashire men were evidently in grand form while it is said the North of Iredand players were not the best that the province might hare afforded. At any rate the visitors proved to be an entirely superior lot and won by six goals to none.

THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY;i APRIL 2a 188 T• _ PROFESSIONAL PROOF. .‘ I WARRINGTON NATIONALISTS AND COERCION. THE lESTINONY 01 THE 'Morons ON A SIMI= Or VITAL IMPORTANCE. On Sunday afternoon a meeting of the Warrington Branch of the Irish National League was held ia the League Hall, Orford-street, in condemnation of the coercive proposals of the Government in regard to Ireland. Ur. F. McLoughlin presided, and there was a good attendance, all earnest and patriotic Irish- .men having been invited to protest against the insult and indignity offered to their country.—The Chair- man, in a brief introductory address, said that they must do all that they could to show their detestation of the monstrous measure proposed to Once more op- press Ireland. He urged Irishmen to join the League, for, he said, it was an organisation that they should be proud to belong to, and one that had it members among the Irish race the world over. No man who knew anything of the history of the last five or six years could say that the League had not done much to advance the cause of Ireland. He was certain that if the coercion Bill was passed it would end—as all Coercion Bille had done—in utter failure, and that Ireland's cause would live long after the Coeroioniets were dead and forgotten. Incidentally he mentioned the assistance being given by English Liberals to the cause of Ireland, and asked those present to attend a mass meeting of Liberals to be held on Saturday next in• the Public Hall.-111r. M. Cuaarnatea proposed the following resolution.—" That we protest In the strongest manner poselble, against the most unjusti- fiable and arbitrary Coercion Bill introduced by the Tory , Government, whose only object seems to be to goad our country into the commission of crime, a design which, we trust, by the patience and forbearance of our poor people will be successfully frustrated, thus demonstrating for the 87th time in as many years the uselessness of coercion as a remedy for the ills of our long-suffering country." The time had new arrived, he added, when they must show that such a thing as coercion would not be allowed te take place. —Mr. J. CHALMERS seconded the resolution. A Coercion Bill for Ireland was in his opinion entirely unnecessary.l What Ireland required was that liberty and freedom that we in England enjoy.—Mr. P. &mimes, of Liverpool, in sup- porting the resolution, described the proposed bill as one at .the most unconstitutional, uncalled for, and cruel measures ever intended for the oppression of a nation. The authors of the bill alleged the prevalence of crime in Ireland as their mason for producing it, and said that such a bill was necese eary in order to put down crime and intimidation, and re- store the country to its normal aspect. It had, however, he contended, been proved beyond the possi- bility of a doubt that crime was no more prevalent in Ire- I land new than it was when in 1885 coercion was declared to be unnecessary. The Conservative Government having obtained office through promises which had since been falsi- fied, were now envious of the power of the National League and of the influence that organisation had upon the Irish people, and had determined to pass the bill in order, not to prevent crime and eviction, but to crush the National League, the national spirit, and convert the Irish teople into a nation of mice who would be afraid to do anything except at the mercy of resident magistrates and the police. (Cheers.) Re believed that the result would prove that the bill was a mistake, and it was for them to see that it should not be a permanent one. The country, after being deceived by the unfulfilled pledges of the Tories at the last election, was steadily coming round in favour of Mr. Gladstone, and was beginning to distrust political quacks of the type of Mr. Chamberlain and others who hal deserted Mr. Gladstone. The Coercion Bill would have the effect of calling out the enthusiasm and earnestness that was in the Irish people, who would chow to the world that they were not to be crushed down. Irish- men would prove that their patriotism was cots thing of mushroom growth, but something immutable and perma- nent, engrafted in their very being, which must remain as long as the last Irishman remained in Ireland. The more they agitated, the more English public opinion, and the public opieion of the whole world, would be with them, and they would create such a wave of opinion as would strike against the very walls of Westminster itself.—Mr. R. O'DosTonnuE, of Liverpool, who also supported the reso- lution, said that Englishmen stood aghast, and were sur- prised that any Government of men calling themselves politicians should dare to introduce a measure so unconsti- tutional and tyrannical as the one the Government were bringing forward. The English people were now recog- nising the true meaning of a Coercion Bill—that the liber- ties of the Irish people were to be taken away by brute force. The Bill was the most ruffianly over proposed for the euppression of the rights and liberties of the people. The fight was not between the people of England and Ire- land, but between the privileged classes and those who were struggling to be free to enjoy the benefits of their own in- dustry. The victory would be to the piople, and they might feel satisfied that Mr. Gladstone would be victorious, and that the day of Ireland's redemption would also see the banner freedom unfurled over the people of this country. —The resolution having been carried with unanimity, the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Imperial White Books " is the title of a new publication by Messrs. Cassell and Co. They are in- tended to be a guide to and summary of public busi- ness; and will include—f, summary of acts of Parlia- ment; 2, summary of bills; 3, summary of reports and tabular statements; 4, index of all Government publications; 5. a list of important letters and speech k ; and (6) references to contemporary publi- cations dealing with the subjects mentioned in the text. From part 1 to hand, we perceive that the "Imperial White Books" will be invaluable to public men for purposes of reference. "The Magazine of Art" for April has for frontis- piece a fine etching of the picture " Under the Charm," painted by Jules Worms. Amongst the more important illustrated articles may be mentioned A boar art revived," " Glimpses of artist life," "Some treasures of the National Gallery," "Van Dyck," and '`Randolph Caldecott." Amongst the most interesting papers in the current issue of " Cas- sell's Magazine" are—" How the Queen travels," "Kitchen physic," "Letters from the planets," and "The roving invalid and hie tiny medicine box." The illustrations are excellent ; they seem to improve every month. "The Quiver," too, is bright with pictures, and is strong in sketch, story, and verse. The Bishop of Ripon has an article on "The work of the Church in Yorkshire," Dr. , Roberts treats of "Groat Biblical scholars," and there is a paper by the Editor on "The Ministry of Angels." " Little Folks" for April is adorned with a coloured frontispiece entitled " Waiting for a game ; " it is really a very pretty picture; but the youngsters are always admirably catered for in this magazine. "The Lady's World" is by this an established favourite with the fair sex. There is an article on " Mrs Gladstone, " as one of the " Ladies of Note," and it is accompanied with a fine portrait from a photograph by the London Stereoscopic Company. The student of " Fashions for April" (illustrated) may soon make herself acquainted with what is taking the lead in London, Paris, Vienna, and Berlin. We have also to hand, from Messrs. Cassell, "False Hopes, or fallacies, socialistic and semi-social- istic, briefly answered by Mr. Goldwin Smith ;" with the current numbers of the Illustrated Shakespeare, Encyclopcedic Dictionary, Gleanings from Popular Authors, and Familiar Wild Flowers. " Scribner's Magazine" for April leads off with a "speaking likeness" of ThackGray, followed by a charming series of his " unpublished letters." Mr. E. B. Washburne concludes his "Reminiscences of the siege and Commune of Paris,'' which are exceed ingly valuable from an historical point of view, and it should be noted that they are capitally illustrated. Other articles and the stories help to constitute an excellent number.

The English Illustrated Magazine" holds its place as the cheapest and best of this class of publi- cations. "The Weedy Moat" is a fine engraving of a fine picture. Ireland, as the "Unknown country," is very readable, ati4 it is for the most part well illus- trated. As much, too, may be saidlor the paper on 'Our Fishermen ;" but the feature of the April num- ber is the true love story of "Sheridan and Miss Linlev." _

- , Part 6 of the new History of Lancashire, published.by ' Mr. John Heywood, carries the reader to chapter nine, and the period of the Wars of the Roses. The issue is adorned with a striking portrait of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster. and several fine engravings of the badges of the House of Lancaster. "Ward and Lock's Technical Journal "leaves no- thing to be desired as to numerous articles and fuLl-page plates. For details of the latest fashions the ladies cannot do better than refer to the issues for April of "The Season" (is), "Le Moniteur de is Mode " (18), " Myr t's Journal" (6d), or to " Myra's Three- penny Journal."
