div.head: INTERNATIONAL BAZAAR AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: INTERNATIONAL BAZAAR AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday afternoon Lord Winmarleigh opened a bazaar, that was arranged on a somewhat extensive scale, in the Drill Hall, at Warrington, its object being to raise money in aid of the build- ing fund in connection with the new and commo- dious schools recently erected in Hamilton-street. A description of the schools, and other particulars regarding them, have been previously given in these columns. They are already in use, supplying a long felt Want, and it was , thought desirable to hold a bazaar in the hope of raising the sum of about .£BOO towards the building fund. The project was entered into with energy, and permission was obtained from the offices of the 18t Volunteer Bat- talion P.W.V., South -Lancashire Regiment, for the use of the Drill Hall, a most suitable room for the purpose. Influential patronage was obtained, and, every effort having been made to ensure success, the 'lnternational Jubilee Bazaar, as it was appropri- ately termed, did credit to its promoters. The stalls, each of' which represented a different coun- try, were arranged round the spacious room, and the fair saleswomen were dressed in a costume illus- tive of the costumes of the countries , represented. In the centre of the room was placed a "fish pond," which was in reality a small space lanced round with plants and flowers, inside which were a number of mysteriouslooking packages, to be angled for by the speculative, and on a stage at the far end of the room Mr. T. J. Down's orchestral band was rocated. In order to secure as good an effect as possible in the arrangement of the stalls and the decorations of the buildings, the services of Messrs. Womersley and Co.. of Leeds, had been requisitioned, and the latest novelties in bazaar fittings secured. Flags of all nations floated on every hand, and the scene 'presented, heightened in effect by the bright looking costumes worn by the stallholders, was a most attractive one. - The work of decoration was carried out under the super- vision of Mr. J. 0. Mason. It may he incidentally mentioned that the designs of the scenery used, when it was presented at the "Paris Exhibition, received a reward' fcr the excellence dl their arrangements. The stalls being arranged round the room, with the small "fish pond" in the centre, left a large space open for the accommodation of the public, and the danger of uncomfortable crowd- ing was thus avoided. Each stall, stocked with articles of all kinds, costly and otherwise, was in itself a bazaar, and it would be impossible to enter into an adequate description of the very large num- ber of articles brought together for sale. The stalls were presided over by the following ladies :—The Oriental: Mrs Stevenson, Mrs McFall, Mrs Langham, and Mrs Adams. The French: Miss Goddard and Miss • Yerriman. Ye Olde Englishe : Mrs William Woods, Mrs Venn Mrs W. S. Woods, Mrs R. Fairclough, and Mrs T. Rojaintlon. The Eng- lish (19th Century) : Mrs Eaude, Mrs Josh. Chrimes, Mrs Cawley, and Miss Whittle. Flower Stall—the Russian : Miss Pierpoint, Miss Cawley. Miss Chrimes, Miss Brookes, Miss Hoult, and Miss Moores. Refreshment Stall—the Swiss: Mrs T. 0. Speakman and Mrs James Smethurst. Increased attraction was added to the affair by the performances on alternate days of the orchestral band of Mr. T. J. Down, and of his military band, each of which con- sists of forty performers. Under Mr. Down's able conductorship, a diversified and brilliant programme of music was discoursed in the afternoon of the opening day, and each evening during the continu- ance of the bazaar. The performances of both these bands were of a very superior character, bearing in mind the large extent in which the amateur ele- ment predominated in each. The music was indeed a theme of general "admiration, and no little credit 'is due to Mr. Down for organising so attractive a contribution to the bazaar. Theatrical representations, variety entertainments. and darlz seances *ere also given at intervals. After the opening ceremony, an excellent group photograph of the saleswomen was taken by Mr. Webster, of Bridge-street. At the ceremony there were a large number of .pliople present, amongst them being, in addition to Lord Winttrarleigh, Mr. Beamont, the Rev. M. Stevenson, the Rev. S. Wil- kinson, the Rev.' G. D. Wray, the Rev. W. H. Wil- liams (Padgate), the Rev. Canon Sharpe, the Rev. J. J. Langham, the Rev. J. A. Drummond, the Rev. Canon Whitley, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Mr. R. Davies, Alderman Harrison, Mr. W. Sharpe, Mr. T. Jolley, Mr. J. Marion, Mr. T. Robinson, the Hon. Miss Wilson Patten, Mr. W. Owen, Mr. J. E. Wright, Dr. Watkins, Alderman Webster, Mr. Francomb, &c, &c. Having been introduced by Mr. Beamont, as one whom they all honoured so much, _
Lord Wxmliatimeat said he had, it the request of some friends and former neighbours, undertaken

to perform the ceremony of opening that bazaar. He did not suppose that when discharging that duty they would expect of him that he should enter upon the merits and demerits of that made of raising fends. Bazaars were now so well known all , through the country that the differences of opinion 1 which existed upon that point some years ago had , ceased; and now it seemed to be held that a bazaar ' was a most legitimate, and, as it seemed, successful mode of raising money for any charitable puipose. He had known in former days very strong opinions , expressed upon the subject, but there was one thing he always observed at the same time, and that was that whatever strong opinions might have been expressed by a friend with regard to bazaars if he wanted to erect schools, to improve a church, or to start a charitable institution, when advertisements had failed, when circular letters were not answered, and when subscriptions did not come in, that friend, whatever his opinions formerly were, himself had recourse to a bazaar. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) By degrees it appeared that all the world came to the same opinion. The reason was perfectly ob- vious, for almost throughout the country these bazaars had been successful. What was the imme- diate cause of success he could not tell them; he did not think it had yet been discovered. It was still amongst the undiscovered parts of science. (Laughter.) But what they cared about were the results, and he could not help hoping and believing that the results as regarded that bazaar would form no exception to the general rule of almost univer- sal success. They might assure themselves that the object of that bazaar deserved every success with which it could meet. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that its purpose was to complete the fund that had been expended in the establishing of elementary schools at the east end of the borough. He dare say that most of those whom he was addressing knew the position of the district in which the schools were placed, but if there was any one whose travels had not led him into those distant regions he was quite sure if he would pro- ceed there he would at once be convinced of the absolute necessity which existed for the establish- ' ing of a school like the one on behalf of which they were there met. He had himself some time ago ' gene through the district, and he had, through the kindness of his young friend Mr. Beamont—(laugh- ter)—been through the school that day, and he was bound to say, although he had had considerable ex- ' perience of schools at different places, that he did not know that he had ever seen a school which he thought was better adapted for the purpose for which it had been built. (Hear, hear.) When he was an inhabitant of the towri, though his in- terest lay in the western ,part of the borough, he al- ways felt that the district of St. Peter's was the most neglected district of the borough. Not that it was not well looked after by the old friends •of theirs who had the superintendence of it, for he be- lieved that no man ever worked harder for the good of the district than the Vicar of St. Peter's—(hear, hear)—but owing to its local position it laboured under very great difficulties. If they looked at the map they would find that tho district was cut off from its happier and more southern members of civilisation—the more southern parts of the bor-• ough—by the long railway that passes through it, and that the people of that district had only com- munication with their happier neighbours on the south through two unimportant arches which give, one more the idea of rabbit holes than the connec- tions between two growing and populous districts, (Hear, hear.) It was a most populous part of the town as they all knew, and the popillation was in- creasing more rapidly than in other districts. Lord Winmarleigh then referred to the circumstances which led to the building of the new schools in Hamilton-street, and he mentioned that although the school had only been opened a short time there were now attending it upwards of 800 children. It would, however, as the district grew in popula- tion accommodate upwards of 800 scholars: (Hear, hear.) He did ' not think that in a meeting of Warrington people it was necessary that he should say very much in favour of education. He had seen a good many. towns, and knew something about the- education within them, but he did not know a town where. more encouragement had been given to education' generally than in the borough of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) In Warrington they had every description of schools—they had their Grammar School, their! Blue Coat School, and their People's College. Theyt had their School of Art, and Museum, and Public Library, and he believed he might say that there was not an inhabitant of the borough of Warring-, ten .who had not the means of preparing himself, at any rete in an, elementarftnentter, for any sta- tion of life to which he chooses to aspire. (Hear, hear.) Many of the greatest characters who had done honour to England in former times had not had the advantages of education which were open to 'every child, every boy, and every I.erson in the borough of Warrington, and he could not think that that school which w.as to form the groundwork of the education of the district in which it is placed would want the supporc which other parts of the town had received from the inhabitants of Warring- ton. As regarded the bazaar he was told It-bad been dot up entirely by the ladies of Warrington. (Applause.). He had often had experience of the benefits derived from the exertions of the ladies of Warritygton, and he did not think they ever en- gaged in a work that did them more credit, and which was more useful to the public than when assisting' that bazaar. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they might see the results he had mentioned, and that the fund which was wanted, and which was only .£BOO, to meet the expenses of the school might be materially aided if not altogether raised by that bazaar. (Applause). On the motion of Mr. BEAMONT, seconded by Dr. WATKINS, a vote of thanks was • heartily ac- corded Lord Winmarleigh. , • ,

div.p: DROWNING iFATALITY AT
WARRINGTON:

Mr. S. Brighouse, county -coroner, held an inquest at the Unicorn Inn, Winwioir-road, on Monday after- noon, on view of the body of John Edward Dyke 3), the son of Samuel Dykes, puddler, 009, Winwick.rd., who was on Saturday afternoon drowned in a clay pit in a briokfield off Winviick-road, belonging to Mr. Edward Bolton.—Samuel Dykes, the father of the de- ceased, said that be last saw his, son alive at about one o'clock on Saturday afternoon. The dead body of his son was brought home the same afternoon. The clay pit was a short distance away from the end of Watkin- street. In answer to the foreman of the jury, witness said that the pit could be fenced round, or the end of the street could be fenced.—john Massey, 23, Ashton-st., a boy, said that he was walking tbroueh the field in question on Saturday, and saw the deceased slip and fall in the water. A man came up with a prop, but could not reach deceased, and a grappling hook having been obtained the body was recovered. There was no person near enough to render assietance when deceased fell in.—ln answer to the Coroner, Inspector Spinks said that there was a depth of seven feet of water in the pit.—James Smith, 34, Watkin- street, said that on Saturday he was at home when he heard a boy was drewned. He went to the pit, where some people were grappling, and jumped in.( He seized hold of the de- , ceased, who was then got out of the water.—Samuel Dykes, ' recalled, said that he and another man tried to restore ani- mation by rubbing deceased for abont ten minutes.—The Coroner said that efforts to restore animation should be con- tinuous for two hours, and remarked that it was a pity the best modes of restoring animation were not more widely known.—Witness said that a number of women who bad Come into the hones pulled him away and teld him he must not do anything till the police or the coroner knew, or he would have taken the clothes off deceased, and the Coroner observed that it was a most absurd idea entertained by some that a person could net be interfered with until the police came.—lnspector Spinks, in answer to the Coroner, said that there had been five or six drowning cases at the spot in questien.—Mr. Newall, who represented the owner of the field, said that Mr. Bolton once went to the expense of erect- ing a paling round the pit, and not a fortnight elapsed:before It was pulled down. They had several times had it repaired, and if had been again and again pulled down.—The Coroner said that the pit was also on Mr. Bolton's private property, and people had no right near it.—The jury returned a verdict te the effect that the deceased was acccidentally drowned.

Mums' CONFERENCE.—A conference of miners' dele- gates from different parts of the country was opened in Manchester on Wednesday. Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., who presided, criticised some of the provisions of the Mines' Regulation Act introduced by the Home Secretary, and afterwards a general discussion on the subject took place. A resolution was passed expressing regret at the undue haste with which the second reading of the Bill was passed through the House of Commons.

Sir,—The interest taken in this movement by the work- ing &Imes in Warrington was shown on Saturday last, when a large number attended a meeting held at the British Workman, liorsemarket-street, from the various works, to consider the best means of forwsrding the movement. Resolutions were passed pledging ourselves to continue the • agitation, i-na laTrender the Free L—el-Tiiig MibiT.ty Corn- mutes all the assistance we possibly can, till this question is brought to a successful issue. It was also proposed to canvass the town from house 9 house and by that means, to get the opinion of all rateßvers sa householders • add if necessary, to have a large demonstrition. -The wolielng classes are determined to have a free lending library. Hoping, the town authorities will see the neopsity ofisolving this' problem, I remain, yours truly, iJoHy sAxotk. , Bewsey-road, Warrington, April 21at, 1887:

THE OVERSEERS OF FRODSHAM LORDSHIP. Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last Iti id there is a let- ter signed "Fair-play." If be means fair play, let him sign his name to his letter or I shall not again trouble to reply. In the first place,he states that the ratepayers' meet- ing at which I was nominated was packed; but I can in- form him that the working-men of Frodsbam are not the people to be packed .like sheen, and " Fair-play " only betrays his ignorance when he ventures to make such a statement. The opinion of a gentleman who was present (and who had attended over thirty Vestry Meetings), was that he never saw so many ratepayers at such a meeting be- fore, nor a meeting better conducted. The meeting was held at a Public House, but that has been a custom from time immemorial, and "Fair-play's " remarks respecting the pints of beer, zbc., seem to be the outcome of his own

muddled brain. His statement that if a poll of the voters had been taken I should not have been in it, simply shows that he knows nothing of Fetedsham Lferdshire and as to my supporters being mostlylciettagers wth bri)y one ,06, I need only rot let " Fair play" to the Editor's remark that we do not guage men either by their titles oo_their money bags. He says that tliiritt trot the first attellal I !have' made to get into office, so I will enlighten him with a few facts. 1. I was elected by the Ratepayers to theriffice of Assesser of Land Tax and when the Collect°, ofrie Tao-wished me to sign the paper without examination, statingwit was the same as it had been for twenty years I refused to do so as I bad a public duty to. perform. 2. The next office I leas' ap- pointed to, bYthe Ratepayers, was what is called a Parochi- al Committeerp! a Sub-sanitary Committee. 3. I was nominated, by' th "ratepayers, by over two votes to one as Waywarden as well as overseer. "Fair-play " hopes I shall profit by my experience. My experience is that the Ratepayers have every confident° or they would not have elected we as they have done to *the various offices mentioned in this letter and as long as it is 'the wish of the Ratepayers that I should hold office I shall .place my servlces at their disposal whatever such meddlina outsiders as " Fair-play " may think, he net having a voiee 'in the matter. It only shows the weakness of my opponents, when tete tave to trust their case in the hands of a man like " Fair- 'play " who is entirely Ignorant of the facts connected thefe- with and has no authority to speak or vote on any subjeoll Connected with the Frodsham Lordship.—Yours truly, JNO. HARGREAVES. River's View, Overton, Frodshamelelth April, 1887. Of I THE CHADLEY CHAIN MAKERS. Sir,—l afilmre .yfiut er,e,what help you possibly. can to the effott abiat to' ge• doclitinliPport ot the poor chain makers of Craitey. I now vilsh, through the "Ex- aminer," to tile affewho sympathise wietrehe victims of these inhum bmpldOets, to 'ine9t ed. the Coffee Tavern, Horsemarket.street, on Saturday evening, at six o'clock. It needs no attelippr on my p?rt to rouse trtie 1:03,98i0ns of War- tington worWeer respectidg this, what.l must call, Cradley ecandal. Can anyone fancy for a moment, what must have been the horrors through which these white slaves have passed during tha past thirty-six weeks? All the misery attending a fireless home, the starving wife, and hungry child. Why, at, it is a wonder the daily papers have not been filled wat,btaccounts,of riot and bloodshed. Yet, when one comes tcothink.aboilt the matter, no wonder the people are quiet. Poverty must have made them spiritless. It has done its. best rwrob the women" of every fetture that adds grace Opd dignity to wemanhood, and for the men— well, I suPPose it is sheer doggedness now, they feel they might just as well stave okaying avterve working. How- ever rnen la ei claire tte being eEngliehmen, members of a liberty loving people. and still persist in all the ac- cursed devicet luvented by the admirers of the "Dismal Sci- ence "passes my comprehension. I keow of no illustra- tion that so aptly points the moral to my recent contribu. tions on trade questions as this one at Cradley. We buy in the cheapest'aed sell in the dearest market. Yee, quite so ; the Cradley employers bay human labour in the cheapest market, and altogether ignore the fact that it is humanity they are dealing in. It is only competition mashed to its logical conclusions ; but at what a sacrifice? Take the following statement, and ponder it over—" The chain-mak- ers Union suffers from the initial drawback that a majority -cif its members are young girls and women, who are more liable than men to be imposed upon by the resolute and art- ful tyranny to which they are exposed." Can year readers discern all the above sentence conveys? Read between the lines; it ought to send a thrill though every Englishwoman that reads it. As for Eneliehmen—well, we remember what they did during the recent wreck of the Victoria. So we need, not wonder that they will bring all the artful ty- renny " to bear on the poor starved wreches at Cradley. Sixty hours for fifteen ebillings, and a strike to maintain it! Sir, the " Examiner " could be filled with incidents Auffieiently inhuman to call forth the strongest proteste.

The s feet of mores, postal communication with the Jl3* • •-• Colonies was again discussed at the-Colonial-Conferenee-on Wednesday. • ' Tan PngsCoT Waxen tnang.—On Monday the Select Committee of the Howie of Commons, appointed to, consider , the bills now before Parliament dealing with merchandise marks, held its first meeting under the presidency of Baron H. De Worms. Two of the bills are promoted by the Board of Trade, one being entitled the Merchandise Marks Actt (1872) Atnendmat Bill, and the other the Merchandise Marks Law Consolidation and Amendment Bill; the third bill, which is introduced by Mr. Mundella, being entitled the Merchandise (Fraudulent Marks) Bill, , In referenc.a to the clauses relating to the watch trade, Mr. Boyle said that strong representations originating at Prescot had been made to the Board. of Trade that foreign made works were placed in English hall-marked cases, and that tha completo watch was thus pissed off as of English mike. The Board had been urged to apply for powers to prohibit entirely the ball. marking of any foreign-made cases, or the placing of foreign-made works in cases marked with the English hall- mark. In the clauses contained in the bill the intention was not to prevent dealers selling English-made cases placed on foreign-made,works or vice versa, but to render it neces- sary thar the exact nature of the whole article should some- how be ascertainable by the purchaser. The name of origin must be stamped on the works, and the assay mark must be stamped on the case. Mr. Boyle mentioned his own CISO to show the kind of fraud that was perpetrated in the watch trade. A friend of his some time ago made him a present of a gold watch which cost 80 guineas. It was described as of English make, and was hall-marked. Some ye as afterwards he placed the watch in the hands of an expert, who at once told him that the works wPre of foreign make, and the watch was only worth £lO —Sir Albert Rol/itt asked whether the system of h..11-marking indicating the quality of gold or silver did not facilitate fraud ?—Witness: Yes, hall-marking has grown up in public °pluton to mean something. that was never intended.--The„committee ad- Owned till Fridiy.

MR. T. C. gDWARDS-MOSS, M.P. ON THR SUNDAY POSTAL DELIVERY. A few days ago the Rev. R. G. Hughes, pastor of the Milton Congregational Chapel, Widnes, *rote to Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for Widnes, in tbs following terms Dear Sir,—As an elector in the district you represent in Parliament, may I ask you to support the motion for releas- ing postmen from Sunday labour to be moved by Dr. Clarke, I believe, on Tuesday, the 19th inst. Those elec- tors in this district to whom fhave spoken on this question are quite in favour of the motion. I shall feel grateful for a reply."—ln acknowledging the communication, Mr. Ed- wards-Moss says—" The. interest that some of my con- stituents take in this question has been brought to toy notice by two petitions which I have presented to the House of Commons for them on this matter. lam glad to be able to Inform you that I am personally quite in sympathy with. the proposal, as I cannot see why, if we in Lon- don can do without a Soodey postal delivery, people in the country should not be able to do so too. Thanking you for milli* Ity attentiOla-to the feeling in Widnes on the point, I remain, yours very faithfully, T. C. PnWILRDS- Mo99.—Rew R. G. Rota's."

Dr. ()Reef:fa proposed the following, motion : Resolved unanimously that we the members of the Widnes Local Board protest against the iniquitous Coercion Act against our Irish fellow subjects now being carried through Parlia- ment, and that a copy of this resolution be sent to the first _Lord of the Treasury.—Mr. Husband asked whether the , Board was qualified to discuss political matters. It was al- ways considered that members of Widnes Local Board were not elected upon political grounds, and that no political matters should be introduced at the Board. He believed that he had heard the chairman already give a decision against the resolution but notwiths.anding that Dr. OKeeffe had taken the liberty of acting contrary to his (the chairman) wishes.—The Chairman said with all respect to • Dr. OKeeffe, he thought that tne subject of that resolution was not one for the Board to seriously consider. They had always been successful in keeping politics out of the pro- ceedings of the Board (hear, hear.) and personally he hoped they would continue to do so. (Applause.)—Mr. Cook: However much we may sympathise with you Doctor. The meeting then terminated.

RUNCORN PRIMROSE LEAGI= The annual meeting of the members of the Runcorn Habitation of the Primrose League was held in the Trinity Schools on Monday night, and there was a modtrate atten- dance. Lady Brook, ruling councillor, presided.--Mr. T. H. Annett reported that there were 50 knights and dames and 516 asseciatei on the books of the society. It-was he added, a matter of deep regret and surprise that the reading manufacturers held aloof from the Habitation. The state- ment of account's showed receipts £56 14s 9d, expeediture £49 4s 6d, leaving a balance in hand of £7 103 3d.—The re- port was adopted oa the motion of the Rev. W. Proton, seconded by Mr. H B Toone.—Lady Brook, alluding teethe formation of the League, said she must really tell the troth about the matter whether Radicals liked it or not. (Laugh- ter.) This division Was so fearfully laulied at for having returned a German at the last election but cue that it went to her heart. (Hear, hear.) She thow;ht that one way of vindicating the honour of the division was to try to establish' a Primrose League. (Applause.) They had met with great difficulties.. The chief people bad not taken up the matter very' warmly, and had not shown them a good ex- ample in working for the Conservative cause. That must, however, be left to their own consciences, but the members of the League were expected to I be warm and active in its work.—Lady Brooke was subse- quently reappointed ruling councillor and Mr. T. H. Annett was re-elected honorary secretary and treasurer, and other routine business having been gone through, Mr. Peter Smith proposed the following reeolution :—The huncorn Habita- tion of the Primrose League humbly desires to convey to the most noble the Marquis of Salisbury, KG., its unabated confidence in his policy, and rejoices in the prospect that ere long the tyranny, coercion, and lawlessness that have so long prevailed in Ireland will give place to the observance of and proper respect for law,. order, and the payment of just debts."—Mr. H. B. Toone seconded the motion, and it was unanimously carried.—On the proposition of Mr. W. H. Rogerson, seconded by Mr. T. Sharrock, a resolution of thanks was accorded to Lord Randolph Churchill for the interest he had taken in the League and for the pitriotic speeches he had lately delivered.—During the evening it was decided to reduce the entrance fee from is to 6d, this amount to include the possession of a badge, which for- merly had to be purchased in addition to the fee.

MR. R. VERDIN, M.P., ON COERCION. Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, the general secretary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association, has received the following letter from Mr. R. Verdin, M.P. for the division, in reply to the resolution passed at a meeting of the District Council a week ago in condemnation of the Coercion Bill : "House of Commons, Wednesday, April 20tb. 1887. Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge receipt of your lettdr of the fifteenth inst., enclosing copy of resolutions passed at a ' District Council meeting of the Liberal Association for the Northwieh Division. I am as desirousas any member of your aseociation that the sympathies of , the Irish peopie should be enlisted on the side of law and order, but we dif- fered at the time of the general election as- to the methods to be employed to ensure that end, and it was for that reason that some who I trust I may still call my friends did not give me their support. I have broken no pledge-that I gave when Aeking election. but I was then and arl now opposed ^ to the coercion on the part of the National Leagnerand regret that it should be found necessary to strengthen the law of the land to protect the weak and the defenceless. The rich man can afford to pay for police protection, but the poor sannot do as, and it is therefore the detv of the state to take measures for the safety of all. —Believe MP, faithfully yours, ROBERT VERDIN. Wm. Handley, Esq., Runcorn." Efforts are being made to hold a public demonstration. in. Runcorn against the Coercion Bill.

Thu anneal meting of this body was held at the ofaces C the Board at Lymm ort.Thursday ovening, for the purpose of electing a chairman,.and transacting other yearly busi- ness. The members present were Messrs Carneron,,the late chairman. Brazendalof Forster, Appleton, H. Harrison, It. Dutton, Rogers, Thomason, with Mr. T. .T.. Ridgwe.y (clerk). - SLECTION OF CESIEGIIIAST.—Mr, Rogers proposed, and 1,6 r. Appleton seconded, that Mr. Cameron be re-elected chair- man of the Board.--.--Mr. Hall rose to propose an amend.- meat. He did not do so, he said, out of any ill-feeling to Mr. Cameron, but because be thought it was not quite fit- ting, and not fair to Mr. Cameron himself,. that he, being the agent of Mt. Dewburst, ahould be chairman of the Locsil Board. If Mr. Cameron had to give a casting, vote it would place him in a very: unfortunate position. If he had to give a casting vote ha would naturally be in favour ' of tbe master from whom he bad to . get his living. He proposed that Mr., Dutton 'be elected chairman. —As the amendment was not seconded,and no other amendment was proposed, the orl.- ginal prnposition was carried.—M. Hall said that it was a most curious thing that Mr, Rogers, who had been rejected by the ratepayers, and who he did not consider a member of tha'a Boarj., should propose the resolution.—Mr. Rogers retorted that he had as.much right on the Board as had any other menfiser. Mr. Hell, as usual, had made a false state- men.--,-Ms-. Hall: Yen were rejected by the ratepayers ; the woukls not have you. You were only pitchforked in.— Ths Chalrkan brioay thanked the Board for their confi- dence. IVith regard to Mr. Hall's fatherly interest in him, and in leis conduct of the business of the Board, he should be the custodian of his own conscience in the management of tho business of the Board. He hoped that he should be , able, if called upon to give a casting vote, to give it fairly, and pointed out that Mr. Hall had never yet been able to lay his finger on one act of his (the chairman's) which he con/d say was unfair to the Board, and he hoped that he should be able to maintain the same pcsition in the future aain the past.—Mr. Hall hoped that the chairman would not think his remarks were made in an unfriendly spirit.— I The matter then dropped, A Co y.—The Chairman read a letter complaining of the state of Booth's-lane. hymm, signed by several resi- dents, who observed that they had concluded to pay no rates until some improvement was made. THE FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT:

Oh Saturday . afternoon a large meeting' of the committee of Working-men, formed for the purpose of promoting the scheme for the freeing of the Lend- ing Library, was held in the Horsemarket-street Cocoa Rooms, Mr. Griffiths presiding. The matter of the-canvassing of the town in furtherance of the scheme' was considered; arid on its being explained that a conference of a sub-committee deputed by the Library Committee; and of the committee appointed at the recent jubilee meeting, was to be held this week for the purpose ce seeing if an arrangement could be' eome to for freeing the rtbrary, it sees decided to defer any further steps as to canvassiagtbe town or holding a demonstration till the results of the conference were known. Mr. A. RATABONB said that when he first received notice to attetd that meeting he was under the im- pression it war in connection with the committee which had beeroappointed from theaTubileemeeting at the Town Hall; the Monday night previous, to wait upon the Museum and library Committee to confer upon the feasibility of making the library a' Free Lending Library. The movement had been again and agasis sneered at as the work of one or two ; busy-bodiess, and it was said that the bulk of the working-class inhabitants of the town didn't care a straw about it. THE STEMS IN TRIX CHAIN , TRADE.— kt a representative meeting of chainmakers, on Thursday, at Cradlew Heath, it was stated that arrangements were being completed fol a, general turnout of all branches, of the trade on Saturday. It: was contended it was necessary to take this extreme course in consequence of a section of the employers syetematically violating the agreement to nay the 4s liat of prices. It is expected Inwards o 5,000 operativoa will lie on strike. MAIRS/ACIE OF LORD, HISRY GROS-MINOR. The marriage of Lord Henry Grosvenor, eldest son of the Duke of Westminster, with Miss riora Mitaa Erskine Weroyes. I daughter of the late Mr. Ames Hay Erskine Weaves, of Werayss and Gerrie, Fife, late M.P. for Fifeshire, took place, , at St. Peter's. Canley Gardens, on Thursday, the officiating I clergy being the Isibn. and Rev. Francis Byng (chaplain to the Speaker). and Rev. Herbert Astley. Amongsethe wed- ding party were the Prince and Princess Christian, the Ductless of Albany, and the Duke and,Do.chess of West- minster.' • THE CREWEMIIRDEE.—Thomas Heary,Devaia the young t man charged with the mureler of his aunt and vaith attempt- lug to murder- his half-sister on the 26th ult., was again I brought before the magistrates at Crewe on Thursday. The iniured girl had now sufficiently recovered from her terrible injuries to be able to give a full narrative of the attack made upon her by the prisoner on her return, after going an errand tuber aunt'a cottage, in wbich she had shortly be- fore left the deceased woman and the prisoaer. Bevan, who, in reply to the charge, simply staid "I did not do it," was committed for trial. A FataNcn 133SERTER.—A Fienchmaa, wearing the uni- form of one of the Hussar regiments of his native country, made his appearance in St. Helens on Saturday night, but coold not make himself understood, beyond the fact that he wanted to speak tea Frenchman. As there was some difis nutty in finding one be was taken to the police office, where a subscription was made for him, and he was quartered at the Eagle and Child Hotel for the night. On Sunday morning be was interrogated by a Frenchman who had been found in Tontine-street, and he then said his name was Alexander Duerst, that ho had assaulted an officer of his regimeut by striking him whilst in a temper, and that be had run away to escape throe years' punishmaat to which he had rendered himself liable. He said lae landed at Dover, had walked to London, from London to Chester, and on to St. Helens and wanted to get to Glasgow, and hoped ultimately to get to America.
